Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale


Contents

1 Overview                                                                                  1

2 Schedule and checkpoints                                                                  3

3 The problem                                                                               3

4 Part 0: Building the cluster                                                              4

5 Part 1: Serial solver                                                                     7

6 Part 2: 1D strip decomposition                                                            7

7 Part 3: 2D block decomposition                                                            9

8 Part 4: Performance study                                                                 9

9 Part 5 (advanced, optional): GPU computing with CUDA                                     10

10 Deliverables                                                                            13

11 Rules                                                                                   14

12 Use of AI and LLMs                                                                      14



1    Overview

In this project your team builds a small distributed-memory cluster out of your own computers
and uses it to simulate heat spreading across a square plate. Each team member runs an Ubuntu
virtual machine; the virtual machines are joined into one private network with Tailscale; and
your solver runs across all of them with MPI.
You will write everything yourselves, starting from the numerical scheme you derived in the
background notes (Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation). The project has the following
parts:

Part 0. Build the cluster. Virtual machines, Tailscale, SSH, Open MPI, and a first measurement
        of what your network can do.

Part 1. Serial solver. A correct, verified C++ implementation of your explicit scheme.

Part 2. 1D strip decomposition. The first parallel version, with halo exchange between
        neighbouring processes.



                                              1
 Part 3. 2D block decomposition. A Cartesian process grid and halo exchange in four
        directions.

Part 4. Performance study. Measure, model and explain how your solver scales on your
        cluster.

Part 5. Advanced (optional): GPU computing with CUDA. Each machine computes its
        part of the plate on its own NVIDIA GPU, while MPI still connects the machines.

  Requirements — background notes
 Every team must complete all the Tasks in the background notes (Numerical Methods
 for the Heat Equation), except those marked optional, and hand in their written solutions.
 Your solver is built on the results of these Tasks, in particular:

           Task       Used in
           3.2, 3.4   second derivative and discrete Laplacian (Part 1)
           5.2        the update rule your solver implements (Parts 1–3, 5)
           5.5        the accuracy you must observe in the convergence study (Part 1)
           6.3        the stability limit your program enforces (Section 3)
           7.2        the convergence study (Part 1)
           8.2        the communication model for strips and blocks (Parts 3 and 4)

 Hand in the solutions as a separate PDF (typed, or neatly handwritten and scanned), numbered
 as in the notes. Tasks that ask for a program or a plot, such as 3.5, 4.1 or 6.7, are answered
 with your results and a short explanation.


Learning objectives

By the end of the project you should be able to:

 set up and debug an MPI environment across several machines;

 decompose a grid-based computation and implement halo exchange;

 verify that a parallel program is correct, not just that it runs;

 measure latency, bandwidth and run time carefully and reproducibly;

 build a simple performance model and use it to explain your measurements, including the cases
  where adding machines makes things slower.

 An honest warning about speed-ups
 Your cluster is connected by home and campus networks through an encrypted overlay. Its
 latency is a thousand times or more worse than that of a real supercomputer interconnect.
 For small grids, your parallel code will very likely run slower on several machines than on one.
 That is not a failure: explaining exactly when and why it happens is one of the main goals of
 the project, and it is worth as much as a good speed-up.




                                                 2
 2    Schedule and checkpoints

Week    Work                                                                           Checkpoint
1       Background-notes Tasks; Part 0 (cluster up, ping-pong measurements) and        C1
        Part 1 (serial solver, convergence study)
2       Part 2 (1D strips), identical output to the serial code                        C2
3       Part 3 (2D blocks) and the performance runs of Part 4                          C3
4       Analysis, report, and live demo                                                Final


Checkpoints are short (10 minutes per team) and ungraded except for a pass/fail on whether you
reached them, but they are where problems get caught early. Bring a laptop that can reach your
cluster.


3    The problem

Solve the 2D heat equation                     2
                                               ∂ u ∂2u
                                                       
                                      ∂u
                                         =α        + 2
                                      ∂t       ∂x2  ∂y
on the unit square [0, 1]2 with α = 1, on a uniform grid of N × N intervals (h = 1/N , nodes
indexed 0 ≤ i, j ≤ N ), using the explicit scheme you derived in Task 5.2 of the background notes.
Your time step must satisfy the stability condition you derived in Task 6.3; it is specified through
the dimensionless parameter r = α ∆t/h2 .
In both simulation cases the plate starts cold, u0 = 0 at every interior node, and heat enters
through edges held at a fixed hot temperature u = 1 (Dirichlet conditions).


Case 1 (four hot edges). All four edges are held at u = 1. Heat flows in from every side and
the plate warms up towards a uniform temperature of 1.


Case 2 (hot top and bottom). The top edge (y = 1) and the bottom edge (y = 0) are held at
u = 1, including the corner nodes; the left and right edges are held at u = 0. The plate approaches
a steady state in which heat flows from the hot edges to the cold ones.


Verification test (V). Cases 1 and 2 have no simple closed-form solution, so correctness is
checked separately on a problem that does: initial condition u0 (x, y) = sin(πx) sin(πy) with u = 0
                                                                              2
on all four edges, whose exact solution is u(x, y, t) = sin(πx) sin(πy) e−2π t . It is used for the
convergence study in Part 1.




                                                 3
     Requirements — program interface
    Your executable heat must accept at least the following options (names may differ; document
    them in your README):

           Option                Meaning                                      Example
           --case                1, 2 or V                                    --case 2
           --N                   number of intervals per direction            --N 1024
           --r                   α∆t/h2                                       --r 0.2
           --T or --steps        final time, or a fixed number of steps       --steps 500
           --out                 output file for the final field (optional)   --out u.bin
           --decomp              serial, strips or blocks                     --decomp blocks

    If --T is given, choose ∆t so that T /∆t is an integer and the requested r is not exceeded. The
    program must refuse to run with an unstable r and say why.

    Requirements — output
     Field file: the full (N + 1) × (N + 1) grid, boundary included, as raw little-endian double
      values in row-major order (row j is the line y = yj ; i varies fastest). No header. The parallel
      versions must write the same file as the serial version, from a single file, regardless of the
      number of processes.

     Standard output: one summary line in key=value form, for example
      decomp=strips P=4 N=2048 steps=500 t total=3.21 t comp=2.10 t comm=1.11
      err inf=...
      (error norms only for test V). This makes it easy to collect results with a script.



4      Part 0: Building the cluster

4.1     Architecture

                         your team’s tailnet (100.x.y.z addresses, encrypted)
                 Alice’s laptop               Bob’s laptop               Carol’s PC



                  Ubuntu VM                      Ubuntu VM                    Ubuntu VM
                  heat-alice                      heat-bob                    heat-carol
                    tailscale0                     tailscale0                   tailscale0


                                              MPI traffic over TCP



Each team member runs one Ubuntu virtual machine. Tailscale inside each VM gives it a stable
private address on your team’s network (your tailnet), even if the machines are in different
buildings, behind different routers, or on Wi-Fi. MPI then treats the VMs as the nodes of a
cluster: mpirun on one VM starts processes on all of them over SSH, and the processes talk to
each other over TCP through Tailscale.




                                                       4
 4.2     Step 1: one VM per machine

 Requirements
  Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS on every VM. All VMs must run the same release so that
   they get the same Open MPI version.

  At least 2 virtual CPUs and 4 GB of RAM per VM, more if you can spare it. Write down
   the host CPU model, the VM’s vCPU count and RAM: you will need them in the report.

  The same user name on every VM (e.g. mpi). MPI starts remote processes as the same
   user and at the same path.

  Default NAT networking is fine: Tailscale handles getting through it.

Any hypervisor works. Multipass (Windows, macOS, Linux) is the quickest; VirtualBox, VMware,
Hyper-V, or UTM on Apple Silicon also work.

 Apple Silicon and mixed architectures
 On an Apple Silicon Mac your VM will be ARM64, while most other laptops are x86-64.
 Open MPI can run across both (they share byte order and type sizes), but: (1) each VM
 must compile its own binary from the same source, at the same path; (2) compile with
 -ffp-contract=off, otherwise the ARM build fuses multiply–adds and produces slightly
 different floating point results; and (3) mention the mix in your report, since nodes of different
 speeds affect load balance.


4.3     Step 2: software
On every VM:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake git openmpi-bin libopenmpi-dev python3-numpy
     python3-matplotlib
mpirun --version        # must print the same version on every VM



4.4     Step 3: the tailnet

One team member creates a Tailscale account; this account owns the team’s tailnet. The free
Personal plan covers a whole team. Then:

1. The owner invites the other team members to the tailnet from the Tailscale admin console.

2. On every VM, install Tailscale and log in, giving each VM a clear hostname:
      curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
      sudo tailscale up --hostname=heat-alice      # use your own name
      tailscale status                              # lists every VM in the tailnet


3. Check that every VM can reach every other one by name (MagicDNS):
      ping -c 3 heat-bob
      tailscale ping heat-bob       # also tells you "direct" or "via DERP"




                                                 5
   Direct or relayed?
 Tailscale first tries to connect two machines directly. When a network blocks that (some
 campus or hotel Wi-Fi), traffic goes through a relay server (DERP ), which adds a lot of
 latency. tailscale ping tells you which one you got. Record it for every pair of machines:
 it will explain some of your measurements.


4.5   Step 4: passwordless SSH

mpirun launches remote processes over SSH, so every VM must be able to log in to every other
VM without a password. Use ordinary OpenSSH keys:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519        # once per VM
ssh-copy-id mpi@heat-bob                                # repeat for every other VM
ssh heat-bob hostname                                   # must work with no prompt at all

Log in once by hand from every VM to every other VM so that the host keys get accepted; a
pending “Are you sure you want to continue connecting?” prompt makes mpirun hang.


4.6   Step 5: the first MPI run
Create a hostfile listing your VMs and how many processes (slots) each may run, normally its
vCPU count:
# hosts
heat-alice slots=2
heat-bob   slots=2
heat-carol slots=4

Tell Open MPI to use the Tailscale interface for both its control channel and its data traffic;
otherwise it may try the VM’s NAT address, which the other machines cannot reach, and hang:
mpirun --hostfile hosts -np 8 \
       --mca oob_tcp_if_include tailscale0 \
       --mca btl_tcp_if_include tailscale0 \
       --mca btl tcp,self \
       hostname

You should see each VM’s name as many times as it has slots. Next, write a “hello world” MPI
program that prints rank, size and host name, build it at the same path on every VM, and run it
the same way.


4.7   Step 6: measuring your network

Before writing the solver, measure what your network can do. Write a ping-pong program: rank 0
sends a message of m bytes to rank 1, which sends it straight back; repeat many times and take
the average round trip. Run it for m = 8 bytes up to 16 MB (powers of two), for

 two processes on the same VM, and
 two processes on different VMs, for every pair of VMs.

Fit the model from Section 8.4 of the background notes, tmsg (m) = ts + m tw , to the one-way
times (half the round trip). The latency ts comes from small messages and the bandwidth 1/tw
from large ones.

                                              6
     Checkpoint: C1 (end of week 1)
     mpirun runs hostname and your hello-world program on all VMs.

     A table of ts and bandwidth for same-VM and every cross-VM pair, with “direct” or “DERP”
      noted.

     Serial solver passing the convergence study (Part 1).

     Written solutions to the background-notes Tasks, at least those listed in Section 1 (the full
      set is due with the final submission).



5      Part 1: Serial solver
    Requirements
     C++17 or later, built with CMake or a Makefile in one command, with -O2 or -O3 and
     -ffp-contract=off.

     The grid stored in one contiguous array (e.g. std::vector<double>), accessed through a
      single indexing function.

     Two arrays for the two time levels, swapped (not copied) after each step (background notes,
      Section 8.2).

     Timing with std::chrono::steady clock or MPI Wtime, of the time-stepping loop only
      (exclude initialization and output).

     Test V reports ∥e∥∞ and ∥e∥2,h against the exact solution at the final time.


Verification. Carry out the convergence study of Task 7.2 in the background notes and include
the completed table and log-log plot in your report. Also do Task 6.7 (deliberately exceed the
stability limit) and include a picture of what happens.
Keep the serial version in the final code (--decomp serial). It is your reference: every parallel
result is checked against it.


6      Part 2: 1D strip decomposition

6.1     Decomposition

Split the N − 1 interior rows among the P processes in contiguous strips, as evenly as possible:
when N − 1 is not divisible by P , the first (N − 1) mod P ranks get one extra row. Rank 0 owns
the bottom strip and rank P − 1 the top one.




                                                  7
                                                                                      rank 3


                                                                                     rank 2
      ghost row (copy of rank 2’s bottom row)

                                                                                     rank 1

          ghost row (copy of rank 0’s top row)
                                                                                     rank 0



Each rank stores its own rows plus one ghost row above and one below (the boundary row of
the plate counts as a ghost row for ranks 0 and P − 1). Local arrays therefore have nlocal + 2 rows
of N + 1 values.


6.2   Halo exchange

At the start of every time step, before computing:

1. send your top owned row to the rank above, and receive into your top ghost row from the rank
   above;
2. send your bottom owned row to the rank below, and receive into your bottom ghost row from
   the rank below.
  Requirements — halo exchange
   Implement the exchange with MPI Sendrecv. Use MPI PROC NULL as the neighbour of ranks
    0 and P − 1 on the outside so that the same code runs on every rank with no special cases.

   Because rows are contiguous in memory, each row is sent as a single message of N + 1
    doubles straight from your array. No packing.

   Time the exchange and the computation separately and report, for each, the maximum over
    ranks (MPI Reduce with MPI MAX).

  Deadlock
  If every rank first calls a blocking MPI Send to its upper neighbour and then MPI Recv, the
  program may work for small N and hang for large N . Explain why in your report, and why
  MPI Sendrecv does not have this problem.


6.3   Output and correctness

Rank 0 assembles the full field (e.g. with MPI Gatherv) and writes it in the format of Section 3,
or all ranks write their part directly with MPI-IO; either is fine.

  Requirements — correctness
 For the same N , r and number of steps, the field file written with --decomp strips on any
 number of processes must be bit-for-bit identical to the serial one (check with cmp). If
 your team mixes x86-64 and ARM VMs, show bit-for-bit equality with all processes on one
 architecture, and report the largest difference on the mixed cluster.


                                                 8
     Debugging a halo exchange
    Run Case 2 with P = 2 and a tiny grid (N = 8), one step, and print the arrays including the
    ghost rows. Then try P = 3 with N = 8 (uneven strips). Off-by-one errors in strip sizes and
    ghost indices are by far the most common bug.

    Checkpoint: C2 (end of week 2)
    Strip version producing output identical to serial for P = 1, 2, 3, 4 and several N (including
    N − 1 not divisible by P ), across at least two VMs.



7      Part 3: 2D block decomposition

Arrange the P processes in a Px × Py grid and give each one a rectangular block of interior nodes.
Each block has ghost layers on all four sides.

    Requirements
     Choose Px , Py with MPI Dims create and build the process grid with MPI Cart create (non-
      periodic). Find neighbours with MPI Cart shift; the edges of the plate are automatically
      MPI PROC NULL.

     Split rows and columns as evenly as possible, as in Part 2.

     Rows of a block are contiguous; columns are not. Send columns using a derived datatype
      built with MPI Type vector, not by copying into a buffer by hand.

     Output identical to serial, as in Part 2.

    Questions to answer in your report
     Corner ghost values are never exchanged. Why doesn’t the 5-point stencil need them?
      Which stencil would?

     For your measured ts and tw , predict from Task 8.2 of the background notes whether strips
      or blocks should be faster for P = 4, 8 and N = 512, 2048, 8192. Then check.


Optional extension. Overlap communication with computation: start the exchange with
MPI Isend/MPI Irecv, update the nodes that do not touch a ghost layer, call MPI Waitall, then
update the nodes next to the ghost layers. Measure whether it helps on your network, and explain
the result.


8      Part 4: Performance study

8.1     Measurement rules

 Use a fixed number of steps (e.g. --steps 500) and r close to your stability limit, so that run
  times are comparable across N .

 Repeat every run at least 3 times and report the median. Note the spread.

 Plug laptops in, close heavy applications, and don’t run anything else in the VMs during
  measurements. Note which machines were on Wi-Fi.


                                                  9
  Do not run more processes on a VM than it has vCPUs.
 Script your runs (bash or Python) and keep the raw output files. The scripts are part of the
  submission.


8.2     Experiments

1. Single-node baseline. Serial run time per step and per grid node on each VM, for N = 512,
   1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192. This gives your compute rate, the other ingredient of the performance
   model.
2. Strong scaling. For N = 512, 2048 and 8192, run strips and blocks with P from 1 up to all your
   slots. Distinguish two placements: processes spread round-robin across VMs (--map-by node),

3. Weak scaling. Keep the work per process fixed (e.g. 1024 × 1024 nodes per process) and grow

of the strip and block versions as a function of N and P (start from Task 8.2 of the background

  Ordinary VMs cannot use the GPU

    once, launch one kernel per time step, swap the two device pointers on the host, and copy
    the result back only at the end. Copying the field back and forth every step would make
    the GPU version slower than the CPU one.

   Check the return value of every CUDA call and check for kernel launch errors
    (cudaGetLastError).

A starting point for the kernel; the update itself is your formula from Task 5.2:
__global__ void step(const double* u_old, double* u_new, int nx, int ny, double r)
{
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // column index
    int j = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;   // row index
    if (i < 1 || i > nx - 2 || j < 1 || j > ny - 2) return; // interior only

}

Combine Step 1 with your strip decomposition from Part 2: one MPI rank per GPU, each rank

    the ghost rows on the GPU, then launch the kernel.

    Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale


Contents

1 Overview                                                                                  1

1    Overview

In this project your team builds a small distributed-memory cluster out of your own computers
and uses it to simulate heat spreading across a square plate. Each team member runs an Ubuntu
virtual machine; the virtual machines are joined into one private network with Tailscale; and
your solver runs across all of them with MPI.
You will write everything yourselves, starting from the numerical scheme you derived in the
background notes (Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation). The project has the following
parts:

Part 0. Build the cluster. Virtual machines, Tailscale, SSH, Open MPI, and a first measurement
        of what your network can do.

Part 1. Serial solver. A correct, verified C++ implementation of your explicit scheme.

Part 2. 1D strip decomposition. The first parallel version, with halo exchange between
        neighbouring processes.



                                              1
 Part 3. 2D block decomposition. A Cartesian process grid and halo exchange in four
        directions.

Part 4. Performance study. Measure, model and explain how your solver scales on your
        cluster.

Part 5. Advanced (optional): GPU computing with CUDA. Each machine computes its
        part of the plate on its own NVIDIA GPU, while MPI still connects the machines.

  Requirements — background notes
 Every team must complete all the Tasks in the background notes (Numerical Methods
 for the Heat Equation), except those marked optional, and hand in their written solutions.
 Your solver is built on the results of these Tasks, in particular:

           Task       Used in
           3.2, 3.4   second derivative and discrete Laplacian (Part 1)
           5.2        the update rule your solver implements (Parts 1–3, 5)
           5.5        the accuracy you must observe in the convergence study (Part 1)
           6.3        the stability limit your program enforces (Section 3)
           7.2        the convergence study (Part 1)
           8.2        the communication model for strips and blocks (Parts 3 and 4)

 Hand in the solutions as a separate PDF (typed, or neatly handwritten and scanned), numbered
 as in the notes. Tasks that ask for a program or a plot, such as 3.5, 4.1 or 6.7, are answered
 with your results and a short explanation.


Learning objectives

By the end of the project you should be able to:

 set up and debug an MPI environment across several machines;

 decompose a grid-based computation and implement halo exchange;

 verify that a parallel program is correct, not just that it runs;

 measure latency, bandwidth and run time carefully and reproducibly;

 build a simple performance model and use it to explain your measurements, including the cases
  where adding machines makes things slower.

 An honest warning about speed-ups
 Your cluster is connected by home and campus networks through an encrypted overlay. Its
 latency is a thousand times or more worse than that of a real supercomputer interconnect.
 For small grids, your parallel code will very likely run slower on several machines than on one.
 That is not a failure: explaining exactly when and why it happens is one of the main goals of
 the project, and it is worth as much as a good speed-up.




                                                 2
 2    Schedule and checkpoints

Week    Work                                                                           Checkpoint
1       Background-notes Tasks; Part 0 (cluster up, ping-pong measurements) and        C1
        Part 1 (serial solver, convergence study)
2       Part 2 (1D strips), identical output to the serial code                        C2
3       Part 3 (2D blocks) and the performance runs of Part 4                          C3
4       Analysis, report, and live demo                                                Final


Checkpoints are short (10 minutes per team) and ungraded except for a pass/fail on whether you
reached them, but they are where problems get caught early. Bring a laptop that can reach your
cluster.


3    The problem

Solve the 2D heat equation                     2
                                               ∂ u ∂2u
                                                       
                                      ∂u
                                         =α        + 2
                                      ∂t       ∂x2  ∂y
on the unit square [0, 1]2 with α = 1, on a uniform grid of N × N intervals (h = 1/N , nodes
indexed 0 ≤ i, j ≤ N ), using the explicit scheme you derived in Task 5.2 of the background notes.
Your time step must satisfy the stability condition you derived in Task 6.3; it is specified through
the dimensionless parameter r = α ∆t/h2 .
In both simulation cases the plate starts cold, u0 = 0 at every interior node, and heat enters
through edges held at a fixed hot temperature u = 1 (Dirichlet conditions).


Case 1 (four hot edges). All four edges are held at u = 1. Heat flows in from every side and
the plate warms up towards a uniform temperature of 1.


Case 2 (hot top and bottom). The top edge (y = 1) and the bottom edge (y = 0) are held at
u = 1, including the corner nodes; the left and right edges are held at u = 0. The plate approaches
a steady state in which heat flows from the hot edges to the cold ones.


Verification test (V). Cases 1 and 2 have no simple closed-form solution, so correctness is
checked separately on a problem that does: initial condition u0 (x, y) = sin(πx) sin(πy) with u = 0
                                                                              2
on all four edges, whose exact solution is u(x, y, t) = sin(πx) sin(πy) e−2π t . It is used for the
convergence study in Part 1.

     Requirements — program interface
    Your executable heat must accept at least the following options (names may differ; document
    them in your README):

           Option                Meaning                                      Example
           --case                1, 2 or V                                    --case 2
           --N                   number of intervals per direction            --N 1024
           --r                   α∆t/h2                                       --r 0.2
           --T or --steps        final time, or a fixed number of steps       --steps 500
           --out                 output file for the final field (optional)   --out u.bin
           --decomp              serial, strips or blocks                     --decomp blocks

    If --T is given, choose ∆t so that T /∆t is an integer and the requested r is not exceeded. The
    program must refuse to run with an unstable r and say why.

    Requirements — output
     Field file: the full (N + 1) × (N + 1) grid, boundary included, as raw little-endian double
      values in row-major order (row j is the line y = yj ; i varies fastest). No header. The parallel
      versions must write the same file as the serial version, from a single file, regardless of the

4      Part 0: Building the cluster

4.1     Architecture

                         your team’s tailnet (100.x.y.z addresses, encrypted)
                 Alice’s laptop               Bob’s laptop               Carol’s PC



                  Ubuntu VM                      Ubuntu VM                    Ubuntu VM
                  heat-alice                      heat-bob                    heat-carol

                                              MPI traffic over TCP



Each team member runs one Ubuntu virtual machine. Tailscale inside each VM gives it a stable
private address on your team’s network (your tailnet), even if the machines are in different
buildings, behind different routers, or on Wi-Fi. MPI then treats the VMs as the nodes of a
cluster: mpirun on one VM starts processes on all of them over SSH, and the processes talk to
each other over TCP through Tailscale.




                                                       4
 4.2     Step 1: one VM per machine

 Requirements
  Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS on every VM. All VMs must run the same release so that
   they get the same Open MPI version.

  At least 2 virtual CPUs and 4 GB of RAM per VM, more if you can spare it. Write down
   the host CPU model, the VM’s vCPU count and RAM: you will need them in the report.

  The same user name on every VM (e.g. mpi). MPI starts remote processes as the same
   user and at the same path.

  Default NAT networking is fine: Tailscale handles getting through it.

Any hypervisor works. Multipass (Windows, macOS, Linux) is the quickest; VirtualBox, VMware,
Hyper-V, or UTM on Apple Silicon also work.

 Apple Silicon and mixed architectures
 On an Apple Silicon Mac your VM will be ARM64, while most other laptops are x86-64.
 Open MPI can run across both (they share byte order and type sizes), but: (1) each VM
 must compile its own binary from the same source, at the same path; (2) compile with
 -ffp-contract=off, otherwise the ARM build fuses multiply–adds and produces slightly
 different floating point results; and (3) mention the mix in your report, since nodes of different
 speeds affect load balance.


4.3     Step 2: software
On every VM:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential cmake git openmpi-bin libopenmpi-dev python3-numpy
     python3-matplotlib
mpirun --version        # must print the same version on every VM



4.4     Step 3: the tailnet

One team member creates a Tailscale account; this account owns the team’s tailnet. The free
Personal plan covers a whole team. Then:

1. The owner invites the other team members to the tailnet from the Tailscale admin console.

2. On every VM, install Tailscale and log in, giving each VM a clear hostname:
      curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
      sudo tailscale up --hostname=heat-alice      # use your own name
      tailscale status                              # lists every VM in the tailnet


3. Check that every VM can reach every other one by name (MagicDNS):
      ping -c 3 heat-bob
      tailscale ping heat-bob       # also tells you "direct" or "via DERP"




                                                 5
   Direct or relayed?
 Tailscale first tries to connect two machines directly. When a network blocks that (some
 campus or hotel Wi-Fi), traffic goes through a relay server (DERP ), which adds a lot of
 latency. tailscale ping tells you which one you got. Record it for every pair of machines:
 it will explain some of your measurements.


4.5   Step 4: passwordless SSH

mpirun launches remote processes over SSH, so every VM must be able to log in to every other
VM without a password. Use ordinary OpenSSH keys:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519        # once per VM
ssh-copy-id mpi@heat-bob                                # repeat for every other VM
ssh heat-bob hostname                                   # must work with no prompt at all

Log in once by hand from every VM to every other VM so that the host keys get accepted; a
pending “Are you sure you want to continue connecting?” prompt makes mpirun hang.


4.6   Step 5: the first MPI run
Create a hostfile listing your VMs and how many processes (slots) each may run, normally its
vCPU count:
# hosts
heat-alice slots=2

8.4     Looking ahead: why and how this parallelizes
Locality. Look at your stencil from Task 5.2(c). Each new value depends only on a handful of
nearby old values. Nothing in one corner of the plate is needed to update the opposite corner
during a single step. This locality is what makes the problem parallel.

Domain decomposition. Split the grid into pieces and give each piece to one process. Within
a step, every process can update all of its interior nodes simultaneously. Only the nodes along
the cut need values owned by a neighbour.

Ghost layers (halos). Each process stores, alongside its own rows, an extra layer of ghost
rows holding copies of its neighbours’ edge values, exactly like the ghost nodes of Example 5.2.
At the start of every time step, processes exchange edge rows to refresh these ghost layers; then
each updates its own nodes with the serial code, unchanged.

Computation versus communication. Per step, a process does work proportional to the
number of nodes it owns (an area) but communicates data proportional to the length of its cut
(a perimeter). A simple model for the time to send a message of m numbers is

                 GPU: sub-domain                              GPU: sub-domain

9.1   Environment

  Ordinary VMs cannot use the GPU
  Multipass, VirtualBox and similar desktop hypervisors do not give the VM access to the host’s
  GPU, so CUDA does not work inside the VMs of Part 0. A machine that takes part in this
  section must instead run its cluster node in one of the following ways:

   Native Ubuntu 24.04 (a lab PC or a dual-boot installation), or

   WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04 on a Windows machine with an NVIDIA GPU. Install only
    the NVIDIA Windows driver; do not install a Linux GPU driver inside WSL2.

  Repeat Part 0 (packages, Tailscale, SSH, same user name) on that node, and check that
  mpirun still reaches it. Machines without an NVIDIA GPU, including all Macs, cannot run
  CUDA; they can stay in the cluster as CPU nodes (Section 9.4).

On each GPU node, install the CUDA toolkit and check that the GPU is visible:
nvidia-smi                          # GPU model, driver and memory
sudo apt install -y nvidia-cuda-toolkit
nvcc --version

NVIDIA’s own CUDA repository provides newer toolkits if you need them. Record the GPU
model, its memory size and its peak memory bandwidth (from the manufacturer’s specifications)
for the report.


9.2   Step 1: a single-GPU solver

  Requirements — single GPU
   Write a CUDA kernel in which each thread updates one interior node, using a 2D
    grid of 2D thread blocks (start with 16 × 16 or 32 × 8 threads per block).

   Allocate both time levels on the GPU with cudaMalloc, copy the initial field to the GPU
    once, launch one kernel per time step, swap the two device pointers on the host, and copy
    the result back only at the end. Copying the field back and forth every step would make
    the GPU version slower than the CPU one.

   Check the return value of every CUDA call and check for kernel launch errors
    (cudaGetLastError).

   Add a --device gpu option. The CUDA code must be optional at build time (e.g. a CMake
    option), so that the project still builds on machines without CUDA.

A starting point for the kernel; the update itself is your formula from Task 5.2:
__global__ void step(const double* u_old, double* u_new, int nx, int ny, double r)
{
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;   // column index
    int j = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;   // row index
    if (i < 1 || i > nx - 2 || j < 1 || j > ny - 2) return; // interior only
    // u_new[j * nx + i] = ... your update rule (Task 5.2) ...
}




                                                11

  Requirements — correctness and timing
   By default nvcc fuses multiply–adds, just like the ARM compiler in Part 0. Compile with
   --fmad=false and show that the GPU output is bit-for-bit identical to the serial CPU
    output. Then report how large the difference is with --fmad=true, and how much faster.

   Time the kernels with CUDA events (cudaEventRecord, cudaEventElapsedTime). Report
    the time per step with and without the initial and final transfers.

   Compute the achieved memory bandwidth: count the bytes your kernel must read and
    write per step, divide by the time per step, and compare with the GPU’s peak bandwidth.
    The stencil does very little arithmetic per byte, so memory bandwidth, not compute, is the
    limit.


9.3   Step 2: one GPU per MPI rank

Combine Step 1 with your strip decomposition from Part 2: one MPI rank per GPU, each rank
keeping its strip, including the ghost rows, in GPU memory.

  Requirements — multi-GPU halo exchange
   The Ubuntu Open MPI package cannot send directly from GPU memory, so stage halos
    through the host. Each step: copy your two boundary rows from the GPU into host buffers
    (cudaMemcpy), exchange them with MPI Sendrecv as in Part 2, copy the received rows into
    the ghost rows on the GPU, then launch the kernel.

   Allocate the host halo buffers with cudaMallocHost (pinned memory) and compare the
    copy times with ordinary malloc’d buffers.

   If a machine has more than one GPU, give each rank on it a different GPU: find the rank’s
    index on its machine with MPI Comm split type(..., MPI COMM TYPE SHARED, ...) and
    pass it to cudaSetDevice.

so write a small kernel that packs a column into a contiguous buffer before the copy, and one that
unpacks it. (b) Overlap: update the interior of the strip in one CUDA stream while the boundary
rows are copied and exchanged in another. (c) A shared-memory version of the kernel, in which
each thread block loads its tile plus a one-node border once; measure whether it beats the simple
kernel on your GPU.


9.4   Mixed CPU and GPU nodes

If only some machines have NVIDIA GPUs, the GPU ranks finish each step much sooner and then
wait for the CPU ranks. Either run the GPU experiments on the GPU nodes only, or implement
a weighted decomposition: measure each node’s time per step on its own, and give each rank
a number of rows proportional to its speed. Report how the waiting time changes.

  From which N is one GPU faster than the CPU of the same machine? Where does the time
   go for small N (kernel launches, transfers)?

  Moving the computation to the GPU makes it much faster, but the network stays the same.
   What happens to the communication share of the run time, and to the point where adding
   a second machine starts to pay off? Answer with your performance model first, then with
   measurements.

   distributed computing over a slow network is worth it?

 the source, building with a single command (cmake + make, or make);

    width table;
(b) the numerical method in brief, with the stability condition and the convergence study;
(c) the design of both decompositions (with a figure), and how you tested them;
(d) the performance results, the model, and the answers to the questions in Parts 3 and 4;
(e) if you attempted Part 5: your GPU setup, the correctness checks, the GPU timings and
    bandwidth, and the answers to its questions;

5. LLM logs. The complete llm log/ folder, including the AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file you
used (Section 12).


6. Live demo (10 minutes). Run Cases 1 and 2 across at least three VMs, on the network
you used for your measurements, and show a heat map or animation of the result. Be ready to
change N or P on request and to explain any part of the code.

11     Rules

 All code must be written by your team, with or without LLM assistance recorded as described
  in Section 12. You may consult MPI documentation and textbooks; cite anything you adapt.

 Your tailnet is your team’s responsibility. Only invite team members, and remove the VMs

You may use AI assistants and large language models (chat assistants, coding agents, code
completion) in this project, under the following conditions.


Record everything

Automate the recording

Numerical Background
Part 1 Solutions:
Task 3.2 - Second derivative
(a) We approximate the second derivative by using the values at the left, center and right points.
D₂f(x) = [f(x − h) − 2f(x) + f(x + h)] / h²
We use the Taylor expansions below. The first-derivative terms cancel when we add them.
f(x + h) = f(x) + hf′(x) + (h²/2)f″(x) + (h³/6)f‴(x) + …
f(x − h) = f(x) − hf′(x) + (h²/2)f″(x) − (h³/6)f‴(x) + …
Adding and rearranging gives the central second-difference formula above.
(b) The leading error is:
D₂f(x) − f″(x) = (h² / 12) f⁽⁴⁾(x) + O(h⁴)
Therefore the approximation is second-order accurate: its main error is proportional to h².
(c) For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 1, the exact value is f″(1) = −sin(1).
h | Absolute error | Error ratio
0.1 | 0.000700992 | -
0.05 | 0.000175292 | 3.999
0.025 | 0.000043826 | 4.000
0.0125 | 0.000010957 | 4.000
When h is halved, the error is about four times smaller. This agrees with second-order accuracy.
Task 3.4 - Discrete Laplacian
(a) Horizontal second derivative:
uₓₓ ≈ [uᵢ₋₁,ⱼ − 2uᵢ,ⱼ + uᵢ₊₁,ⱼ] / (Δx)²
(b) Vertical second derivative:
uᵧᵧ ≈ [uᵢ,ⱼ₋₁ − 2uᵢ,ⱼ + uᵢ,ⱼ₊₁] / (Δy)²
(c) Add the two formulas to approximate the Laplacian, ∇²u = uₓₓ + uᵧᵧ. The error is O((Δx)² + (Δy)²).
(d) When Δx = Δy = h, we obtain the five-point formula:
∇²ₕuᵢ,ⱼ ≈ [Left + Right + Top + Bottom − 4 × Center] / h²
(e) The stencil uses the center and four neighbors. Its weights, before division by h², are:
                         +1
                +1       −4       +1
                         +1
(f) If the neighbor average is larger than the center value, the Laplacian is positive and heat tends to raise the center temperature. This agrees with the mean-value interpretation.
Task 5.2 - Update rule for the heat equation
The heat equation is uₜ = α(uₓₓ + uᵧᵧ). We use Forward Euler for time and the discrete Laplacian for space.
(a) For different horizontal and vertical spacings:
uⁿ⁺¹ᵢ,ⱼ = uⁿᵢ,ⱼ + αΔt [ (Left − 2Center + Right)/(Δx)²
                                 + (Bottom − 2Center + Top)/(Δy)² ]
(b) With equal spacing h, define r = αΔt/h². Then:
New center = (1 − 4r) × Center + r × (Left + Right + Top + Bottom)
This is the equation implemented in our C++ serial solver.
(c) The space-time stencil uses five values at old time n to calculate one center value at new time n + 1:
Time n:   Left, Right, Top, Bottom, Center   →   Time n + 1: New center
Fixed boundary nodes are not updated.
(d) With coefficients already calculated, one update needs about 6 floating-point operations, 5 input values and 1 output value. Actual memory traffic can be lower because neighboring values are reused from cache.
Task 5.5 - Accuracy and consistency
Our method makes two types of approximation: Forward Euler in time and central differences in space.
Forward Euler is first-order in time. The spatial formulas are second-order. So the local truncation error is:
τ = O(Δt) + O((Δx)²) + O((Δy)²)
Therefore p = 1 and q = 2.
The method is consistent because the truncation error approaches zero when Δt, Δx and Δy approach zero. Consistency alone does not guarantee stability.
Task 6.3 - Stability condition
(a) Von Neumann analysis studies how a Fourier-shaped numerical error changes after one time step. Write the error as Gⁿ exp[i(jθ + kφ)]. Substituting it into the update rule gives:
G(θ, φ) = 1 − 4rₓ sin²(θ/2) − 4rᵧ sin²(φ/2)
rₓ = αΔt/(Δx)²,      rᵧ = αΔt/(Δy)²
(b) A stable scheme requires |G| ≤ 1 for every error mode. The worst high-frequency mode is the alternating checkerboard (θ = φ = π). Its factor is:
Gworst = 1 − 4rₓ − 4rᵧ
Requiring Gworst ≥ −1 gives the general stability condition:
αΔt [1/(Δx)² + 1/(Δy)²] ≤ 1/2
(c) If Δx = Δy = h, then rₓ = rᵧ = r, so:
Gworst = 1 − 8r        and        0 ≤ r ≤ 0.25
(d) For equal spacing, the stability limits are r ≤ 1/2 in 1D, r ≤ 1/4 in 2D and r ≤ 1/6 in 3D.
Task 6.7 - Deliberate instability test
We deliberately exceeded the 2D stability bound by 5%: r = 1.05 × 0.25 = 0.2625, with N = 16 and Case V.
For the worst mode, G = 1 − 8(0.2625) = −1.1. Its sign changes from step to step and its magnitude grows by 10% per step.

100 | 0.001854518

Written solutions to Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 of Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Chapter 8 (pp. 24–26). The communication model also prepares Parts 3 and 4.
Task 8.1 - Why not update in place?
(a) Assume that we visit the rows from bottom to top (increasing j), and the points within each row from left to right (increasing i). For an interior point away from physical boundaries, the left neighbour (i−1, j) and the bottom neighbour (i, j−1) have already been updated to level n+1. The right and top neighbours still contain level n values. Fixed boundary values do not change.
(b) No. The explicit scheme requires all five values to come from the old time level:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r[uⁿ(i−1,j) + uⁿ(i+1,j) + uⁿ(i,j−1) + uⁿ(i,j+1)]
Updating in place mixes two time levels. For example, the first updated point can affect the next point during the same sweep. Reversing the sweep changes which neighbours contain new values and can change the numerical result.
(c) Order-independence is essential in parallel because different ranks update their strips concurrently. If the stencil reads partially updated values, the result can depend on the order of operations, the timing of messages and the partition of the grid. With two arrays, every rank reads only level n, writes level n+1, and swaps the arrays at the end of the step. Ghost rows must also contain level n values. The same arithmetic then produces the same result regardless of the order in which points are updated.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
The notes use an ideal N × N grid split evenly among P processes. Assume that N is divisible by P for strips, and that P is a perfect square and N is divisible by √P for square blocks. We count a typical interior rank with all its neighbours. Physical-edge ranks communicate less.
(a) Strips
Each rank owns N/P rows of N values, so it computes N²/P points. It sends one row of N values to each of two neighbours, and receives one row of N values from each.
Sent = 2N numbers; received = 2N numbers; total = 4N numbers.
There are 2 outgoing messages and 2 incoming messages per step (4 individual send/receive events).
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume (continued)
(b) Square blocks
The ranks form a √P × √P process grid. Each rank owns a square block of side N/√P and area N²/P. An interior rank has four neighbours. The five-point stencil requires only the four edge halos, not diagonal corner messages.
Sent = 4N/√P; received = 4N/√P; total = 8N/√P numbers.
There are 4 outgoing messages and 4 incoming messages per step (8 individual send/receive events).
(c) Communication time per step
The notes give the message model t_msg = tₛ + m t_w, where tₛ is start-up latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t_w is the transfer time per value. We use the usual per-rank model counting one bidirectional exchange per neighbour, with matching send and receive treated as one message cost. We neglect overlap between different neighbour exchanges.
T_comm,strips ≈ 2(tₛ + Nt_w) = 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
T_comm,blocks ≈ 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t_w) = 4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P
If sends and receives are charged separately rather than as paired exchanges, both estimates are doubled; the comparison is unchanged under that convention.
When latency is small, the data volume dominates. Blocks transfer less data than strips for P > 4 in this interior-rank model. When latency is very large, strips are preferable because they require fewer messages.
More precisely, the block estimate is smaller when:
4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P < 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
tₛ < Nt_w(1 − 2/√P)
Thus blocks need a sufficiently large data volume and a sufficiently low latency to compensate for their additional messages. For small process grids, count the actual neighbours rather than applying the interior-rank formula blindly.
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio for strips
Let γ be the average computation time per point per step. A typical rank owns N²/P points, so:
T_comp ≈ γN²/P
T_comm / T_comp ≈ (2tₛ + 2Nt_w)/(γN²/P)
T_comm / T_comp ≈ 2Ptₛ/(γN²) + 2Pt_w/(γN)
For fixed P, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term as 1/N. Larger grids therefore provide more computation per exchanged value. On a slow network, parallelism is more likely to pay off for large problems, although speedup is not guaranteed by this model alone.
Application to our Part 2 implementation
The project uses N intervals per direction, not exactly the N × N point grid used in Task 8.2. It has (N+1)² total points and (N−1)² updated interior points. The number of rows owned by a rank is determined by the balanced strip partition.
q = ⌊(N−1)/P⌋,     s = (N−1) mod P
n_local(k) = q+1 if k < s; otherwise q.
Each rank stores (n_local+2)(N+1) doubles. The extra rows are ghost rows or physical boundary rows. An actual halo message contains N+1 contiguous doubles (8(N+1) bytes on the tested machines). An interior rank has two MPI neighbours; the first and last ranks have only one when P > 1.
Example: N = 16, P = 3
Here there are 15 interior rows and each rank owns 5. Each rank stores 7 × 17 = 119 doubles per time-level array and updates 5 × 15 = 75 interior temperatures per step. A halo message contains 17 doubles, or 136 bytes.

Connection to the implementation
At every step, MPI_Sendrecv refreshes the ghost rows in the old array before computation. The five-point update writes into the new array, then the arrays are swapped. Part 1: Serial solver and verification
We implemented the serial reference solver for the two-dimensional heat equation on the unit square. It supports Case 1 (four hot edges), Case 2 (hot top and bottom, cold sides), and verification Case V (zero boundaries with a known exact solution).
Numerical method
The plate is represented by a uniform grid with spacing h = 1/N, including its boundary nodes. We use Forward Euler in time and a five-point central-difference stencil in space (α = 1). At each interior node, the temperature is updated by:
u(new) = (1 − 4r)u(center) + r[u(left) + u(right) + u(top) + u(bottom)]
Here r = Δt / h². The explicit method is stable for 0 < r ≤ 0.25. When a final time T is requested, the solver adjusts the number of steps and Δt so that the final time is reached without exceeding the requested r.
Implementation and output
The C++17 solver uses two contiguous double arrays, a single row-major indexing function and an array swap after each iteration. Boundary values are held fixed. It builds with one Makefile command using -O2 and -ffp-contract=off. std::chrono::steady_clock measures only the update loop, excluding initialization and file output. The program prints a one-line key=value summary and, when requested, writes the full (N+1) × (N+1) grid as raw doubles in row-major order.
Correctness and convergence
Cases 1 and 2 were checked at N = 8, r = 0.2 and 20 steps. Both produced finite temperatures between 0 and 1 with the prescribed edge values. For Case V, the exact solution is sin(πx)sin(πy)exp(−2π²t). We report the maximum error and the discrete L2,h error at the final time.
The convergence study used T = 0.05, r = 0.2 and N = 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256. Doubling N reduced both error norms by approximately four, with observed orders close to 2 (2.0058 to 2.0001 for L2,h). This matches the expected O(Δt + h²) accuracy, since Δt = rh². The complete table and log-log plot are in Appendix D.
Stability test
The normal solver rejects r > 0.25. A separate test program deliberately used r = 0.2625 (5% above the limit). The maximum error grew from 6.07 × 10⁻⁴ at 400 steps to 1.30 at 500 steps and 6.19 × 10¹⁶ at 1,000 steps. The final field shows alternating positive and negative temperatures in a checkerboard pattern, consistent with the unstable high-frequency amplification factor G = 1 − 8r = −1.1. Figures and data appear in Appendix E.
The serial mode remains the reference for future numerical comparisons with the strip and block decompositions. Its integration into the final combined executable will be checked when those parallel modes are added.

Part 4: Performance study
We measured the serial, MPI strips and MPI blocks solvers on the three Ubuntu VMs (two vCPUs and 4 GB RAM each). The benchmark used Case 2, r = 0.24 and 10 fixed time steps. The short run length was chosen because of repeated network interruptions; it increases sensitivity to timing noise. Three repetitions were planned per configuration, with median and min–max spread reported. No performance run used oversubscription. MPI was configured for TCP over Tailscale, including local MPI ranks.
Single-node baseline and scaling
All 45 serial runs completed for N = 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192. At N = 8192, median times were 1.050 s (heat-1), 2.023 s (heat-2) and 0.718 s (heat-3). The cluster is heterogeneous. Strong scaling was completed locally for all three required grid sizes and across machines for several configurations. At N = 8192, local strips achieved 1.79× speedup with P = 2, using the first recorded baseline batch. For N = 512, cross-machine execution was much slower and communication share exceeded 97% for P = 3–5. Weak scaling was measured locally at P = 1 and 2; the three P = 3 strips runs with heat-3 also completed, pending raw-log verification of the clipped timings. See Appendices A–D.
Performance model and required questions
Crossover: no measured cross-machine configuration demonstrated a benefit over the corresponding heat-2 serial baseline at N = 512 or 2048. The placement-aware model predicts a benefit over local P = 2 at N = 8192 (heat-2 + heat-1); distributed N = 8192 remains pending. The model assumes fixed per-link latency and bandwidth and per-node computation cost. It substantially underestimates measured times; variable Wi-Fi, relays, synchronization, heterogeneity and cache effects are possible contributors.
With a hypothetical 1 µs cross-machine startup latency and unchanged bandwidth, predicted P = 4 blocks time falls from 48.32 ms to 13.21 ms at N = 512 (10 steps). This is a sensitivity calculation, not a real cluster measurement. For Tailscale, we recommend stable direct links, wired networking where possible, local execution for small grids, and careful rank placement and repeated measurements.
Pending experiments and limitations
The remaining strong-scaling slot and node runs and distributed weak-scaling runs are PENDING. MPI repeatedly froze, SSH/Tailscale connectivity was intermittent, and LAN diagnostics showed a peer TCP connection failure. Repeated attempts and 30–120 s timeouts prevented completion. ### Numerical_Solutions_Simple.docx pages 4 images 2 equations 0 lines 99
Numerical Background
Part 1 Solutions:
Task 3.2 - Second derivative
(a) We approximate the second derivative by using the values at the left, center and right points.
D₂f(x) = [f(x − h) − 2f(x) + f(x + h)] / h²
We use the Taylor expansions below. The first-derivative terms cancel when we add them.
f(x + h) = f(x) + hf′(x) + (h²/2)f″(x) + (h³/6)f‴(x) + …
f(x − h) = f(x) − hf′(x) + (h²/2)f″(x) − (h³/6)f‴(x) + …
Adding and rearranging gives the central second-difference formula above.
(b) The leading error is:
D₂f(x) − f″(x) = (h² / 12) f⁽⁴⁾(x) + O(h⁴)
Therefore the approximation is second-order accurate: its main error is proportional to h².
(c) For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 1, the exact value is f″(1) = −sin(1).
h | Absolute error | Error ratio
0.1 | 0.000700992 | -
0.05 | 0.000175292 | 3.999
0.025 | 0.000043826 | 4.000
0.0125 | 0.000010957 | 4.000
When h is halved, the error is about four times smaller. This agrees with second-order accuracy.
Task 3.4 - Discrete Laplacian
(a) Horizontal second derivative:
uₓₓ ≈ [uᵢ₋₁,ⱼ − 2uᵢ,ⱼ + uᵢ₊₁,ⱼ] / (Δx)²
(b) Vertical second derivative:
uᵧᵧ ≈ [uᵢ,ⱼ₋₁ − 2uᵢ,ⱼ + uᵢ,ⱼ₊₁] / (Δy)²
(c) Add the two formulas to approximate the Laplacian, ∇²u = uₓₓ + uᵧᵧ. The error is O((Δx)² + (Δy)²).
(d) When Δx = Δy = h, we obtain the five-point formula:
∇²ₕuᵢ,ⱼ ≈ [Left + Right + Top + Bottom − 4 × Center] / h²
(e) The stencil uses the center and four neighbors. Its weights, before division by h², are:
                         +1
                +1       −4       +1
                         +1
(f) If the neighbor average is larger than the center value, the Laplacian is positive and heat tends to raise the center temperature. This agrees with the mean-value interpretation.
Task 5.2 - Update rule for the heat equation
The heat equation is uₜ = α(uₓₓ + uᵧᵧ). We use Forward Euler for time and the discrete Laplacian for space.
(a) For different horizontal and vertical spacings:
uⁿ⁺¹ᵢ,ⱼ = uⁿᵢ,ⱼ + αΔt [ (Left − 2Center + Right)/(Δx)²
                                 + (Bottom − 2Center + Top)/(Δy)² ]
(b) With equal spacing h, define r = αΔt/h². Then:
New center = (1 − 4r) × Center + r × (Left + Right + Top + Bottom)
This is the equation implemented in our C++ serial solver.
(c) The space-time stencil uses five values at old time n to calculate one center value at new time n + 1:
Time n:   Left, Right, Top, Bottom, Center   →   Time n + 1: New center
Fixed boundary nodes are not updated.
(d) With coefficients already calculated, one update needs about 6 floating-point operations, 5 input values and 1 output value. Actual memory traffic can be lower because neighboring values are reused from cache.
Task 5.5 - Accuracy and consistency
Our method makes two types of approximation: Forward Euler in time and central differences in space.
Forward Euler is first-order in time. The spatial formulas are second-order. So the local truncation error is:
τ = O(Δt) + O((Δx)²) + O((Δy)²)
Therefore p = 1 and q = 2.
The method is consistent because the truncation error approaches zero when Δt, Δx and Δy approach zero. Consistency alone does not guarantee stability.
Task 6.3 - Stability condition
(a) Von Neumann analysis studies how a Fourier-shaped numerical error changes after one time step. Write the error as Gⁿ exp[i(jθ + kφ)]. Substituting it into the update rule gives:
G(θ, φ) = 1 − 4rₓ sin²(θ/2) − 4rᵧ sin²(φ/2)
rₓ = αΔt/(Δx)²,      rᵧ = αΔt/(Δy)²
(b) A stable scheme requires |G| ≤ 1 for every error mode. The worst high-frequency mode is the alternating checkerboard (θ = φ = π). Its factor is:
Gworst = 1 − 4rₓ − 4rᵧ
Requiring Gworst ≥ −1 gives the general stability condition:
αΔt [1/(Δx)² + 1/(Δy)²] ≤ 1/2
(c) If Δx = Δy = h, then rₓ = rᵧ = r, so:
Gworst = 1 − 8r        and        0 ≤ r ≤ 0.25
(d) For equal spacing, the stability limits are r ≤ 1/2 in 1D, r ≤ 1/4 in 2D and r ≤ 1/6 in 3D.
Task 6.7 - Deliberate instability test
We deliberately exceeded the 2D stability bound by 5%: r = 1.05 × 0.25 = 0.2625, with N = 16 and Case V.
For the worst mode, G = 1 − 8(0.2625) = −1.1. Its sign changes from step to step and its magnitude grows by 10% per step.
Time steps | Maximum absolute error
100 | 0.001854518
300 | 0.0000954815
400 | 0.000607306
500 | 1.303888
600 | 2,822.024
1,000 | 6.192109 × 10¹⁶
The error becomes very large after about 400-500 steps. The 1,000-step image shows alternating positive and negative values, called a checkerboard pattern.
Measured unstable temperature field after 1,000 steps (r = 0.2625).
The strongest oscillations in this final image are near the center. To identify exactly where instability first became visible, the intermediate saved grids still need to be inspected.
Task 7.1 - Expected convergence order
We know that the error behaves as O(Δt) + O(h²). During our tests we kept r fixed, so Δt = rh²/α.
Therefore the total leading error behaves as O(h²). We expect second-order convergence: halving h should make the error about four times smaller.
Task 7.2 - Convergence study
(a) We ran the serial solver for Case V with T = 0.05 and r = 0.2, at N = 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256.
The exact solution is u(x, y, t) = sin(πx) sin(πy) exp(−2π²t).
(b) The recorded errors were:

64 | 1/64 | 1,024 | 0.000103442 | 0.0000517212 | 2.0014
128 | 1/128 | 4,096 | 0.0000258542 | 0.0000129271 | 2.0004
256 | 1/256 | 16,384 | 0.00000646314 | 0.00000323157 | 2.0001
The observed order is calculated by:
pobs = log₂ [Error(h) / Error(h/2)]
Log-log graph of the discrete L2,h error against grid spacing h.
(c) The observed order approaches 2. This agrees with Task 7.1 and supports the correctness of our serial implementation.

### Part2_Numerical_Solutions_Simple.docx pages 3 images 0 equations 0 lines 55
Numerical Background - Part 2 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Written solutions to Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 of Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Chapter 8 (pp. 24–26). The communication model also prepares Parts 3 and 4.
Task 8.1 - Why not update in place?
(a) Assume that we visit the rows from bottom to top (increasing j), and the points within each row from left to right (increasing i). For an interior point away from physical boundaries, the left neighbour (i−1, j) and the bottom neighbour (i, j−1) have already been updated to level n+1. The right and top neighbours still contain level n values. Fixed boundary values do not change.
(b) No. The explicit scheme requires all five values to come from the old time level:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r[uⁿ(i−1,j) + uⁿ(i+1,j) + uⁿ(i,j−1) + uⁿ(i,j+1)]
Updating in place mixes two time levels. For example, the first updated point can affect the next point during the same sweep. Reversing the sweep changes which neighbours contain new values and can change the numerical result.
(c) Order-independence is essential in parallel because different ranks update their strips concurrently. If the stencil reads partially updated values, the result can depend on the order of operations, the timing of messages and the partition of the grid. With two arrays, every rank reads only level n, writes level n+1, and swaps the arrays at the end of the step. Ghost rows must also contain level n values. The same arithmetic then produces the same result regardless of the order in which points are updated.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
The notes use an ideal N × N grid split evenly among P processes. Assume that N is divisible by P for strips, and that P is a perfect square and N is divisible by √P for square blocks. We count a typical interior rank with all its neighbours. Physical-edge ranks communicate less.
(a) Strips
Each rank owns N/P rows of N values, so it computes N²/P points. It sends one row of N values to each of two neighbours, and receives one row of N values from each.
Sent = 2N numbers; received = 2N numbers; total = 4N numbers.
There are 2 outgoing messages and 2 incoming messages per step (4 individual send/receive events).
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume (continued)
(b) Square blocks
The ranks form a √P × √P process grid. Each rank owns a square block of side N/√P and area N²/P. An interior rank has four neighbours. The five-point stencil requires only the four edge halos, not diagonal corner messages.
Sent = 4N/√P; received = 4N/√P; total = 8N/√P numbers.
There are 4 outgoing messages and 4 incoming messages per step (8 individual send/receive events).
(c) Communication time per step
The notes give the message model t_msg = tₛ + m t_w, where tₛ is start-up latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t_w is the transfer time per value. We use the usual per-rank model counting one bidirectional exchange per neighbour, with matching send and receive treated as one message cost. We neglect overlap between different neighbour exchanges.
T_comm,strips ≈ 2(tₛ + Nt_w) = 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
T_comm,blocks ≈ 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t_w) = 4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P
If sends and receives are charged separately rather than as paired exchanges, both estimates are doubled; the comparison is unchanged under that convention.
When latency is small, the data volume dominates. Blocks transfer less data than strips for P > 4 in this interior-rank model. When latency is very large, strips are preferable because they require fewer messages.
More precisely, the block estimate is smaller when:
4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P < 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
tₛ < Nt_w(1 − 2/√P)
Thus blocks need a sufficiently large data volume and a sufficiently low latency to compensate for their additional messages. For small process grids, count the actual neighbours rather than applying the interior-rank formula blindly.
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio for strips
Let γ be the average computation time per point per step. A typical rank owns N²/P points, so:
T_comp ≈ γN²/P
T_comm / T_comp ≈ (2tₛ + 2Nt_w)/(γN²/P)
T_comm / T_comp ≈ 2Ptₛ/(γN²) + 2Pt_w/(γN)
For fixed P, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term as 1/N. Larger grids therefore provide more computation per exchanged value. On a slow network, parallelism is more likely to pay off for large problems, although speedup is not guaranteed by this model alone.
Application to our Part 2 implementation
The project uses N intervals per direction, not exactly the N × N point grid used in Task 8.2. It has (N+1)² total points and (N−1)² updated interior points. The number of rows owned by a rank is determined by the balanced strip partition.
q = ⌊(N−1)/P⌋,     s = (N−1) mod P
n_local(k) = q+1 if k < s; otherwise q.
Each rank stores (n_local+2)(N+1) doubles. The extra rows are ghost rows or physical boundary rows. An actual halo message contains N+1 contiguous doubles (8(N+1) bytes on the tested machines). An interior rank has two MPI neighbours; the first and last ranks have only one when P > 1.
Example: N = 16, P = 3
Here there are 15 interior rows and each rank owns 5. Each rank stores 7 × 17 = 119 doubles per time-level array and updates 5 × 15 = 75 interior temperatures per step. A halo message contains 17 doubles, or 136 bytes.
Rank | Owned rows | Sent / received per step | Messages sent / received
0 | 1–5 | 17 / 17 doubles | 1 / 1
1 | 6–10 | 34 / 34 doubles | 2 / 2
2 | 11–15 | 17 / 17 doubles | 1 / 1
The three-VM Case V experiment on 24 November 2026 used these parameters, r=0.2 and 10 steps. The measured MPI time was 0.779550588 s, with maximum communication time 0.779543372 s and maximum computation time 0.000008195 s. The serial and distributed fields matched byte for byte. These timings demonstrate communication dominance for this small experiment; they do not establish a general speedup threshold. Timing maxima are independent across ranks.
Connection to the implementation
At every step, MPI_Sendrecv refreshes the ghost rows in the old array before computation. The five-point update writes into the new array, then the arrays are swapped. MPI_Gatherv reconstructs the full field at the end. This implements the order-independence from Task 8.1 and the strip communication pattern from Task 8.2.
Document scope
This document covers both required tasks in Chapter 8. It complements the Part 1 numerical solutions and is not yet the complete project-wide background-notes submission. The final submission must contain all non-optional tasks, numbered as in the notes.
Sources: Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 (pp. 24–26); Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale, Section 6 (pp. 7–9); recorded three-VM Case V verification, 24 November 2026.

### Part3_Numerical_Solutions_Simple.docx pages 3 images 0 equations 0 lines 65
Numerical Background - Part 3 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Task 8.2 (a–d), Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, p. 26; and the two report questions in the project specification, Section 7.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
(a) Strip decomposition
Consider an N × N grid divided into P horizontal strips. Each process owns N/P rows of N points. A typical interior process has two neighbors. It sends its top and bottom rows and receives one row from each neighbor.
Sent: 2N values in 2 messages; received: 2N values in 2 messages.
In total, it exchanges 4N values in 4 directional messages per step. The amount of computation is proportional to N²/P owned points.
(b) Square block decomposition
For a square process grid, each block has side length N/√P. A typical interior process has four neighbors and sends one row or column to each neighbor. It also receives four corresponding ghost layers.
Sent: 4N/√P values in 4 messages; received: 4N/√P values in 4 messages.
The total exchange is 8N/√P values in 8 directional messages. The computation per process is again proportional to N²/P. These counts assume a process with all four neighbors; boundary ranks have fewer.
(c) Communication time per step
The message model is tₘₛɢ = tₛ + m t𝑤, where tₛ is startup latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t𝑤 is the transfer time per value. We estimate the halo cost using the sum of outgoing message costs, rather than adding a second full cost for simultaneous receives.
Tstrips = 2(tₛ + N t𝑤) = 2tₛ + 2N t𝑤
Tblocks = 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t𝑤) = 4tₛ + (4N/√P)t𝑤
With small latency, square blocks reduce the transfer volume for P > 4. With very large latency, strips have the advantage of fewer messages. Under the typical interior-rank model, blocks are faster when:
tₛ < N t𝑤(1 − 2/√P)
This is a simplified communication model, not a guarantee of actual wall-clock performance. In particular, a non-periodic 2 × 2 grid has no four-neighbor rank.
Task 8.2 (continued)
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio
Let t꜀ be the time needed to update one interior point. Each strip owns approximately N²/P points. Therefore:
Tcomp = (N²/P)t꜀
Tcomm / Tcomp = (2tₛ + 2N t𝑤) / [(N²/P)t꜀]
Tcomm / Tcomp = 2P tₛ/(N²t꜀) + 2P t𝑤/(N t꜀)
With P fixed, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term decreases as 1/N. Both approach zero as N increases. Large problems can therefore provide a better balance of computation and communication over a slow network. This does not prove a speedup by itself, since the hardware and MPI implementation also affect performance.
Part 3 report question 1 - Corner ghost values
The explicit five-point stencil computes the next temperature using the center and its four direct neighbors:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r(L + R + B + T)
No diagonal term is present. Even for an owned point at the corner of a block, the required neighbors are in its own block or its adjacent ghost row and column. Hence the corner ghost cells are never read by the stencil and do not need to be exchanged. A nine-point stencil with diagonal terms would require them.
Part 3 report question 2 - Actual process grids
Our non-periodic Cartesian grids use (Py, Px) = (2, 2) for P = 4 and (4, 2) for P = 8. We also consider P = 6, with (Py, Px) = (3, 2), because our three VMs currently have two vCPUs each.
For the busiest strip rank, there are two row messages of length approximately N. For blocks, a rank sends rows of length N/Px and columns of length N/Py to its existing neighbors. We approximate N−1 interior points by N; our actual strip messages contain N+1 doubles.

performance_model.py """Part 4 / Section 8.3: approximate per-rank computation + outgoing halo model.
Inputs: recorded Part 0 network fit, serial medians, confirmed parallel repetitions.
The placement is expected from the hostfile, not a captured rank map.
"""
import csv, math, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
D=Path(__file__).resolve().parent
with (D/'network_inputs.csv').open() as f:
    network={tuple(sorted((r['host_a'],r['host_b']))):(float(r['latency_ms'])*1e-3,8/(float(r['bandwidth_MB_s'])*1e6)) for r in csv.DictReader(f)}
with (D/'serial_inputs.csv').open() as f:
    tc={(r['host'],int(r['N'])):float(r['median_seconds'])/(10*(int(r['N'])-1)**2) for r in csv.DictReader(f)}
with (D/'parallel_inputs.csv').open() as f:
    groups={}
    for r in csv.DictReader(f):
        key=r['dataset'],int(r['N']),int(r['P']),r['method']
        groups.setdefault(key,[]).append(float(r['t_total_s'])/10)
def split(n,p,k): return n//p+(k<n%p)
def dims(P):
    px=math.isqrt(P)
    while P%px: px-=1
    return P//px,px

def prediction(N,P,method,placement,hosts,latency_override=None):
    ranks=([h for h in hosts for _ in range(2)] if placement=='slot' else list(hosts)*2)[:P]
    py,px=(P,1) if method=='strips' else dims(P)
    parts=[]
    for i,host in enumerate(ranks):
        y,x=divmod(i,px)
        nx,ny=split(N-1,px,x),split(N-1,py,y)
        comp=nx*ny*tc[host,N]
        comm=0.
        for yy,xx,m in [(y-1,x,N+1 if method=='strips' else nx),(y+1,x,N+1 if method=='strips' else nx),(y,x-1,ny),(y,x+1,ny)]:
            if 0<=yy<py and 0<=xx<px:
                other=ranks[yy*px+xx]
                ts,tw=network[tuple(sorted((host,other)))]
                if latency_override is not None and host!=other: ts=latency_override
                comm+=ts+m*tw
        parts.append((comp+comm,comp,comm,i))
    return max(parts)
rows=[]
for dataset,hosts,maps,Ns,Ps in [('part4_slot',('heat-2','heat-1','heat-3'),('slot','node'),(512,2048,8192),range(1,7)),('part3_two_vm',('heat-2','heat-3'),('slot',),(512,2048,8192),(4,))]:
    for mapby in maps:
        for N in Ns:
            for P in Ps:
                for method in ('strips','blocks'):
                    pred,comp,comm,rank=prediction(N,P,method,mapby,hosts)
                    vals=groups.get((dataset,N,P,method),[]) if mapby=='slot' else []
                    med=statistics.median(vals) if len(vals)==3 else None
                    rows.append(dict(dataset=dataset,N=N,P=P,method=method,placement=mapby,predicted_step_s=pred,critical_rank=rank,rank_compute_s=comp,rank_communication_s=comm,confirmed_runs=len(vals),measured_median_step_s=med,measured_min_step_s=min(vals) if vals else None,measured_max_step_s=max(vals) if vals else None))
with (D/'performance_model.csv').open('w',newline='') as f:
    w=csv.DictWriter(f,fieldnames=rows[0]);w.writeheader();w.writerows(rows)
for dataset,filename,xfield,title,flt in [
    ('part4_slot','model_vs_measured_N512.png','P','N=512 | slot placement | heat-2, heat-1, heat-3',lambda r:r['N']==512 and r['placement']=='slot'),
    ('part3_two_vm','model_vs_measured_P4_amer.png','N','P=4 | slot placement | heat-2 + heat-3',lambda r:True)]:
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,5.4))
    for method in ('strips','blocks'):
        rr=sorted([r for r in rows if r['dataset']==dataset and r['method']==method and flt(r)],key=lambda r:r[xfield])
        line,=ax.plot([r[xfield] for r in rr],[1000*r['predicted_step_s'] for r in rr],ls='--',marker='o',label=f'{method.title()} model')
        mm=[r for r in rr if r['measured_median_step_s'] is not None]
        y=[r['measured_median_step_s']*1000 for r in mm]
        ax.errorbar([r[xfield] for r in mm],y,yerr=[[v-r['measured_min_step_s']*1000 for v,r in zip(y,mm)],[r['measured_max_step_s']*1000-v for v,r in zip(y,mm)]],fmt='s-',capsize=4,color=line.get_color(),label=f'{method.title()} measured median (min–max)')
    ax.set_yscale('log'); ax.set_xlabel('MPI processes P' if xfield=='P' else 'Grid size N'); ax.set_ylabel('Time per step (ms, log scale)');ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks(sorted({r[xfield] for r in rr}));
    if xfield=='N': ax.set_xscale('log',base=2); ax.set_xticks([512,2048,8192],['512','2048','8192'])
    ax.grid(True,which='both',alpha=.22); ax.legend(fontsize=8);fig.tight_layout();fig.savefig(D/filename,dpi=200);plt.close(fig)
for r in rows:
    if r['dataset']=='part4_slot' and r['placement']=='slot' and r['N']==512 or r['dataset']=='part3_two_vm':
        print(r['dataset'],r['N'],r['P'],r['method'],round(r['predicted_step_s']*1000,4),None if r['measured_median_step_s'] is None else round(r['measured_median_step_s']*1000,4))
