body(report, 'The convergence plotting script reads the recorded solver output in results/convergence_runs.txt and regenerates the table and plot.')
commands(report, './heat --decomp serial --case 1 --N 64 --r 0.2 --steps 100 \\\n'
    '    --out results/demo_case1.bin\n'
    './heat --decomp serial --case 2 --N 64 --r 0.2 --steps 100 \\\n'
    '    --out results/demo_case2.bin\n'
    './heat --decomp serial --case V --N 16 --r 0.2625 --steps 1000')
body(report, 'The last command checks that the stable solver rejects r = 0.2625 with an error message.')
commands(report, 'make unstable_demo\n'
    './unstable_demo --case V --N 16 --r 0.2625 --steps 1000 \\\n'
    '    --out results/instability_1000.bin\n'
    'python3 scripts/plot_instability.py')
body(report, 'The tables and figures use the Part 1 solver logs and verification fields. The test definitions are given in the project specification, Section 5, and in Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Tasks 6.7 and 7.2.')
report.save(output / 'Part1_Report_Copy_Ready.docx')

numerical = new_document('Part 1 Numerical solutions')
numerical.add_heading('Part 1 Numerical solutions', 0)
body(numerical, 'These solutions derive the serial heat update, its stability limit, and its expected convergence order. The Case V results verify the predicted second-order convergence when the time step scales with h².')

heading(numerical, 'Task 3.2 Central second difference')
body(numerical, '(a) Add the Taylor expansions at x + h and x − h. The odd powers cancel.')
equation(numerical, 'f(x + h) + f(x − h) = 2f(x) + h² f″(x) + (h⁴/12) f⁽⁴⁾(x) + O(h⁶)')
body(numerical, '(b) Subtract 2f(x) and divide by h². The leading error is proportional to h², so the approximation is second-order accurate.')
equation(numerical, 'D₂f(x) = [f(x − h) − 2f(x) + f(x + h)] / h²')
equation(numerical, 'D₂f(x) − f″(x) = (h²/12) f⁽⁴⁾(x) + O(h⁴)')
body(numerical, '(c) For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 1, compare D₂f(1) with the exact value −sin(1).')
data_table(numerical, ('h', 'Absolute error', 'Previous error divided by current error'), [
    ('0.1', '0.000700992', '—'), ('0.05', '0.000175292', '3.999'),
    ('0.025', '0.000043826', '4.000'), ('0.0125', '0.000010957', '4.000'),
], (1.05, 1.78, 3.42))

heading(numerical, 'Task 3.4 Discrete Laplacian')
body(numerical, '(a–c) Apply the central second difference separately along x and y, then add the two approximations.')
equation(numerical, 'D_{xx}u = [u(i−1,j) − 2u(i,j) + u(i+1,j)] / Δx²')
equation(numerical, 'D_{yy}u = [u(i,j−1) − 2u(i,j) + u(i,j+1)] / Δy²')
body(numerical, 'The sum approximates ∇²u with error O(Δx² + Δy²).')
body(numerical, '(d–e) With Δx = Δy = h, the stencil below is divided by h².')
commands(numerical, '                 +1\n'
    '          +1     −4     +1\n'
    '                 +1')
body(numerical, '(f) The formula is 4/h² times the neighboring average minus the center. A center cooler than its neighbors gives a positive Laplacian. This is the same local comparison as the mean-value formula.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 5.2 Explicit two dimensional update', page=True)
body(numerical, '(a) Forward Euler in time and the discrete Laplacian in space give the update at an interior node.')
equation(numerical, 'uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = uⁿ(i,j) + αΔt [D_{xx}uⁿ(i,j) + D_{yy}uⁿ(i,j)]')
body(numerical, '(b) For equal spacing h, define r = αΔt/h². The center coefficient is 1 − 4r, and each of the four neighbors has weight r.')
equation(numerical, 'uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r[uⁿ(i−1,j) + uⁿ(i+1,j) + uⁿ(i,j−1) + uⁿ(i,j+1)]')
body(numerical, '(c) The stencil takes all five inputs from level n and writes one center value at level n + 1.')
commands(numerical, 'Old level n                          New level n + 1\n'
    '          Top\n'
    'Left     Center     Right    ────>        Center\n'
    '         Bottom')
body(numerical, '(d) With the coefficients precomputed, one update takes three additions to sum the neighbors, two multiplications and one final addition. It reads five grid values and writes one. Neighboring updates can reuse values in cache.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 5.5 Truncation error and consistency')
body(numerical, 'Insert the smooth exact solution into the discrete equation. Define τ as the forward time difference minus α times the two centered space differences. Taylor expansion at the current node and time gives')
equation(numerical, 'Forward time difference = uₜ + (Δt/2)uₜₜ + O(Δt²)')
equation(numerical, 'D_{xx}u = u_{xx} + (Δx²/12)u_{xxxx} + O(Δx⁴)')
equation(numerical, 'D_{yy}u = u_{yy} + (Δy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δy⁴)')
body(numerical, 'The leading time derivative and Laplacian terms cancel because the exact solution satisfies the heat equation. The leading terms that remain are')
equation(numerical, 'τ = (Δt/2)uₜₜ − (αΔx²/12)u_{xxxx} − (αΔy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δt² + Δx⁴ + Δy⁴).')
body(numerical, 'Therefore τ = O(Δt) + O(Δx²) + O(Δy²), so p = 1 and q = 2. The truncation error tends to zero as the time step and the grid spacings shrink. The scheme is consistent.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 6.3 Two dimensional stability')
body(numerical, '(a) Substitute the mode Gⁿ exp[i(jθ + kφ)]. A shift by one node multiplies the mode by exp(±iθ) or exp(±iφ). Pairing the shifts gives the sine-squared form below.')
equation(numerical, 'G = 1 − 4r_{x} sin²(θ/2) − 4r_{y} sin²(φ/2),  r_{x} = αΔt/Δx²,  r_{y} = αΔt/Δy²')
body(numerical, '(b) G is at most 1 and is smallest for θ = φ = π, the alternating mode. Requiring that minimum to be at least −1 gives the stability condition.')
equation(numerical, 'αΔt(1/Δx² + 1/Δy²) ≤ 1/2')
body(numerical, '(c–d) For equal spacing, the bound is r ≤ 1/4 in 2D. Each direction can contribute −4r to G. In d dimensions the minimum is 1 − 4dr, which gives 1/2 in 1D and 1/6 in 3D.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 6.7 Deliberate instability', page=True)
body(numerical, 'We ran Case V at N = 16 and r = 0.2625, which is 5% above the 2D stability limit. The Fourier bound gives G = 1 − 8r = −1.1 for the ideal alternating mode. The minus sign reverses the mode each step and |G| > 1 amplifies it.')
body(numerical, 'At 300 steps the maximum error was still small. In the saved 400-step field, the new oscillations are most visible in the interior near the plate center. At 500 steps the maximum error exceeds 1, and at 1,000 steps the checkerboard dominates the field. The snapshots show the region where instability became visible without resolving its exact onset step.')
instability_table(numerical, 'Maximum absolute error at the saved step counts.')
figure(numerical, intermediate_plot, 5.68, 'Error fields at 400 and 500 steps. Each panel has its own color scale.',
       'Intermediate error fields show oscillations growing in the interior near the center.')
figure(numerical, final_plot, 3.28, 'Temperature field after 1,000 steps at r = 0.2625.',
       'Final field shows an alternating grid-scale checkerboard with very large signed values.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 7.1 Expected convergence order', page=True)
body(numerical, 'Task 5.5 gives error terms of order Δt and h². Keeping r fixed makes Δt = rh²/α, so both terms scale as h². For the stable, smooth verification problem we expect second-order convergence in h. Halving h should reduce the error by about a factor of four.')

heading(numerical, 'Task 7.2 Convergence study')
body(numerical, '(a) The serial solver ran Case V to T = 0.05 for N = 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256 with r = 0.2. At each of these grid sizes, T/(rh²) is an integer and r is below the stability limit.')
body(numerical, '(b) At T we compared each grid with the exact field sin(πx) sin(πy) exp(−2π²T). We report the maximum absolute nodal error and the discrete L₂ error, h times the square root of the sum of squared nodal errors.')
convergence_table(numerical, 'Measured Case V errors and observed L₂ orders.')
figure(numerical, convergence_plot, 6.20, 'Log-log plot of the two measured errors against grid spacing h, with a second-order reference line.',
       'The measured maximum and discrete L2 errors decrease in parallel with an order-two trend.')
body(numerical, '(c) Using p = log₂[E(h)/E(h/2)] for the discrete L₂ error, the orders approach 2 from 2.0058 to 2.0001. The measured behavior agrees with the prediction in Task 7.1.')
body(numerical, 'Sources. Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Tasks 3.2, 3.4, 5.2, 5.5, 6.3, 6.7, 7.1, and 7.2. The measured values and plots come from the Part 1 solver logs and verification fields.')
numerical.save(output / 'Part1_Numerical_Solutions.docx')
print('\n'.join(str(p) for p in sorted(output.glob('*.docx'))))

'@ | & "$dep/python/python.exe" -

import csv
import math
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

results = Path("results")
rows = []

# Read the actual output of the five solver runs
for line in (results / "convergence_runs.txt").read_text().splitlines():
    if not line.startswith("decomp=serial"):
        continue

    values = dict(item.split("=", 1) for item in line.split() if "=" in item)
    N = int(values["N"])

    rows.append({
        "N": N,
        "h": 1.0 / N,
        "steps": int(values["steps"]),
        "max_error": float(values["err_inf"]),
        "l2h_error": float(values["err_l2h"]),
    })

rows.sort(key=lambda row: row["N"])

assert [row["N"] for row in rows] == [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]

# Calculate observed order of convergence
for i, row in enumerate(rows):
    row["p_obs"] = "" if i == 0 else math.log2(
        rows[i-1]["l2h_error"] / row["l2h_error"]
    )

# Save the completed table
with (results / "convergence.csv").open("w", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=rows[0].keys())
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)

# Plot measured error and theoretical second-order reference
h = [row["h"] for row in rows]
errors = [row["l2h_error"] for row in rows]
reference = [errors[0] * (x / h[0])**2 for x in h]

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.loglog(h, errors, "o-", label="Measured L2 error")
plt.loglog(h, reference, "--", label="Reference: order 2")
plt.xlabel("Grid spacing h")
plt.ylabel("L2 error")
plt.title("Serial Heat Solver - Convergence")
plt.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(results / "convergence.png", dpi=200)

print("N     Observed order")
for row in rows:
    p = row["p_obs"]
    print(f'{row["N"]:<5} {p:.4f}' if p != "" else f'{row["N"]:<5} -')

print("Saved results/convergence.csv")
print("Saved results/convergence.png")

content.text:
# Appendix F Reproducing the serial tests

Start in the part1 directory on Ubuntu, using Bash. The plotting scripts need Python 3 and Matplotlib. Each run saves its results in a new temporary folder.

## Build both programs

make heat unstable_demo\
 part1="$PWD"\
 run_dir=$(mktemp -d)\
 cd "$run_dir"\
 mkdir results

## Case V convergence

for N in 16 32 64 128 256; do\
     "$part1/heat" --case V --N "$N" --r 0.2 --T 0.05\
 done > results/convergence_runs.txt\
 python3 "$part1/scripts/plot_convergence.py"



The script reads the new log and creates convergence.csv and a log-log plot of the discrete L₂ error. The observed order should approach 2.

## Fixed boundaries and stability check

for c in 1 2; do\
     "$part1/heat" --case "$c" --N 8 --r 0.2 --steps 20 --debug\
 done\
 "$part1/heat" --case V --N 16 --r 0.2625 --steps 1000



The printed grids show the fixed boundaries and temperatures in [0, 1]. The final command is expected to fail because r = 0.2625 exceeds the stable limit.

## Deliberate instability

demo_args=(--case V --N 16 --r 0.2625)\
 for n in 100 300 400 500 600 1000; do\
     field="results/instability\_$n.bin"\
     log="results/instability\_$n.txt"\
     "$part1/unstable_demo" "${demo_args[@]}" --steps "$n" --out "$field" > "$log"\

from hot regions to cold ones. The rate and direction of that flow is described by the heat flux q,
a vector whose magnitude is energy per unit time per unit area (W/m2 ).

  In an isotropic material the heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient and points
  down it:
                                            q = −k ∇T,
  where k > 0 is the thermal conductivity of the material, in W/(m·K). In one dimension this
  reads q = −k ∂T /∂x.

    The minus sign encodes the everyday observation that heat flows from hot to cold: if T
increases to the right, ∂T /∂x > 0, and the flux is negative (to the left).

2.5      Linear recurrences
Many numerical methods, applied to simple problems, reduce to a recurrence of the form
xn+1 = g xn , with g a real or complex number. Its solution is xn = g n x0 , so:

 if |g| < 1, then xn → 0;

 if |g| = 1, then |xn | = |x0 | for all n;

 if |g| > 1, then |xn | → ∞ exponentially fast;

 if g < 0 (real), the sign of xn alternates from step to step.

The number g is called the amplification factor. This elementary fact is the heart of stability
theory.

Stability and Convergence

6.1    Consistency is not enough
A consistent scheme reproduces the PDE as the grid is refined, but this alone does not guarantee
that its solution approaches the PDE’s solution. Small errors (truncation errors, round-off) are
made at every node at every step. If the scheme amplifies them, they grow exponentially and
swamp the answer, exactly as forward Euler did on the test equation with λ∆t > 2.

  Definition 6.1. (Stability and convergence)
 A scheme is stable if the size of its numerical solution (in some norm) is bounded in terms
 of the size of its initial data, uniformly for all sufficiently small ∆t, ∆x, ∆y satisfying any
 stated restriction between them. It is convergent if the numerical solution at any fixed time
 T tends to the exact solution as the grid is refined.

 Theorem 6.2. (Lax equivalence theorem)
  For a consistent finite difference scheme approximating a well-posed linear initial value
  problem,
                                  stability ⇐⇒ convergence.

   The theorem turns a hard question (does the scheme converge?) into two easier ones: is it
consistent (Task 5.5), and is it stable (this chapter)?

Locality. Look at your stencil from Task 5.2(c). Each new value depends only on a handful of
nearby old values. Nothing in one corner of the plate is needed to update the opposite corner
during a single step. This locality is what makes the problem parallel.

Domain decomposition. Split the grid into pieces and give each piece to one process. Within
a step, every process can update all of its interior nodes simultaneously. Only the nodes along
the cut need values owned by a neighbour.

Ghost layers (halos). Each process stores, alongside its own rows, an extra layer of ghost
rows holding copies of its neighbours’ edge values, exactly like the ghost nodes of Example 5.2.
At the start of every time step, processes exchange edge rows to refresh these ghost layers; then
each updates its own nodes with the serial code, unchanged.

number of nodes it owns (an area) but communicates data proportional to the length of its cut
(a perimeter). A simple model for the time to send a message of m numbers is

Part2_Numerical_Solutions_Simple.docx
Numerical Background - Part 2 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Written solutions to Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 of Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Chapter 8 (pp. 24–26). The communication model also prepares Parts 3 and 4.
Task 8.1 - Why not update in place?
(a) Assume that we visit the rows from bottom to top (increasing j), and the points within each row from left to right (increasing i). For an interior point away from physical boundaries, the left neighbour (i−1, j) and the bottom neighbour (i, j−1) have already been updated to level n+1. The right and top neighbours still contain level n values. Fixed boundary values do not change.
(b) No. The explicit scheme requires all five values to come from the old time level:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r[uⁿ(i−1,j) + uⁿ(i+1,j) + uⁿ(i,j−1) + uⁿ(i,j+1)]
Updating in place mixes two time levels. For example, the first updated point can affect the next point during the same sweep. Reversing the sweep changes which neighbours contain new values and can change the numerical result.
(c) Order-independence is essential in parallel because different ranks update their strips concurrently. If the stencil reads partially updated values, the result can depend on the order of operations, the timing of messages and the partition of the grid. With two arrays, every rank reads only level n, writes level n+1, and swaps the arrays at the end of the step. Ghost rows must also contain level n values. The same arithmetic then produces the same result regardless of the order in which points are updated.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
The notes use an ideal N × N grid split evenly among P processes. Assume that N is divisible by P for strips, and that P is a perfect square and N is divisible by √P for square blocks. We count a typical interior rank with all its neighbours. Physical-edge ranks communicate less.
(a) Strips
Each rank owns N/P rows of N values, so it computes N²/P points. It sends one row of N values to each of two neighbours, and receives one row of N values from each.
Sent = 2N numbers; received = 2N numbers; total = 4N numbers.
There are 2 outgoing messages and 2 incoming messages per step (4 individual send/receive events).

Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume (continued)
(b) Square blocks
The ranks form a √P × √P process grid. Each rank owns a square block of side N/√P and area N²/P. An interior rank has four neighbours. The five-point stencil requires only the four edge halos, not diagonal corner messages.
Sent = 4N/√P; received = 4N/√P; total = 8N/√P numbers.
There are 4 outgoing messages and 4 incoming messages per step (8 individual send/receive events).
(c) Communication time per step
The notes give the message model t_msg = tₛ + m t_w, where tₛ is start-up latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t_w is the transfer time per value. We use the usual per-rank model counting one bidirectional exchange per neighbour, with matching send and receive treated as one message cost. We neglect overlap between different neighbour exchanges.
T_comm,strips ≈ 2(tₛ + Nt_w) = 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
T_comm,blocks ≈ 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t_w) = 4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P
If sends and receives are charged separately rather than as paired exchanges, both estimates are doubled; the comparison is unchanged under that convention.
When latency is small, the data volume dominates. Blocks transfer less data than strips for P > 4 in this interior-rank model. When latency is very large, strips are preferable because they require fewer messages.
More precisely, the block estimate is smaller when:
4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P < 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
tₛ < Nt_w(1 − 2/√P)
Thus blocks need a sufficiently large data volume and a sufficiently low latency to compensate for their additional messages. For small process grids, count the actual neighbours rather than applying the interior-rank formula blindly.
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio for strips
Let γ be the average computation time per point per step. A typical rank owns N²/P points, so:
T_comp ≈ γN²/P
T_comm / T_comp ≈ (2tₛ + 2Nt_w)/(γN²/P)
T_comm / T_comp ≈ 2Ptₛ/(γN²) + 2Pt_w/(γN)
For fixed P, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term as 1/N. Larger grids therefore provide more computation per exchanged value. On a slow network, parallelism is more likely to pay off for large problems, although speedup is not guaranteed by this model alone.

Application to our Part 2 implementation
The project uses N intervals per direction, not exactly the N × N point grid used in Task 8.2. It has (N+1)² total points and (N−1)² updated interior points. The number of rows owned by a rank is determined by the balanced strip partition.
q = ⌊(N−1)/P⌋,     s = (N−1) mod P
n_local(k) = q+1 if k < s; otherwise q.
Each rank stores (n_local+2)(N+1) doubles. The extra rows are ghost rows or physical boundary rows. An actual halo message contains N+1 contiguous doubles (8(N+1) bytes on the tested machines). An interior rank has two MPI neighbours; the first and last ranks have only one when P > 1.
Example: N = 16, P = 3
Here there are 15 interior rows and each rank owns 5. Each rank stores 7 × 17 = 119 doubles per time-level array and updates 5 × 15 = 75 interior temperatures per step. A halo message contains 17 doubles, or 136 bytes.
The three-VM Case V experiment on 24 November 2026 used these parameters, r=0.2 and 10 steps. The measured MPI time was 0.779550588 s, with maximum communication time 0.779543372 s and maximum computation time 0.000008195 s. The serial and distributed fields matched byte for byte. These timings demonstrate communication dominance for this small experiment; they do not establish a general speedup threshold. Timing maxima are independent across ranks.
Connection to the implementation
At every step, MPI_Sendrecv refreshes the ghost rows in the old array before computation. The five-point update writes into the new array, then the arrays are swapped. MPI_Gatherv reconstructs the full field at the end. This implements the order-independence from Task 8.1 and the strip communication pattern from Task 8.2.
Document scope
This document covers both required tasks in Chapter 8. It complements the Part 1 numerical solutions and is not yet the complete project-wide background-notes submission. The final submission must contain all non-optional tasks, numbered as in the notes.
Sources: Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 (pp. 24–26); Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale, Section 6 (pp. 7–9); recorded three-VM Case V verification, 24 November 2026.

Numerical Background - Part 3 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Task 8.2 (a–d), Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, p. 26; and the two report questions in the project specification, Section 7.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
(a) Strip decomposition
Consider an N × N grid divided into P horizontal strips. Each process owns N/P rows of N points. A typical interior process has two neighbors. It sends its top and bottom rows and receives one row from each neighbor.
Sent: 2N values in 2 messages; received: 2N values in 2 messages.
In total, it exchanges 4N values in 4 directional messages per step. The amount of computation is proportional to N²/P owned points.
(b) Square block decomposition
For a square process grid, each block has side length N/√P. A typical interior process has four neighbors and sends one row or column to each neighbor. It also receives four corresponding ghost layers.
Sent: 4N/√P values in 4 messages; received: 4N/√P values in 4 messages.
The total exchange is 8N/√P values in 8 directional messages. The computation per process is again proportional to N²/P. These counts assume a process with all four neighbors; boundary ranks have fewer.
(c) Communication time per step
The message model is tₘₛɢ = tₛ + m t𝑤, where tₛ is startup latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t𝑤 is the transfer time per value. We estimate the halo cost using the sum of outgoing message costs, rather than adding a second full cost for simultaneous receives.
Tstrips = 2(tₛ + N t𝑤) = 2tₛ + 2N t𝑤
Tblocks = 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t𝑤) = 4tₛ + (4N/√P)t𝑤
With small latency, square blocks reduce the transfer volume for P > 4. With very large latency, strips have the advantage of fewer messages. Under the typical interior-rank model, blocks are faster when:
tₛ < N t𝑤(1 − 2/√P)
This is a simplified communication model, not a guarantee of actual wall-clock performance. In particular, a non-periodic 2 × 2 grid has no four-neighbor rank.

Task 8.2 (continued)
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio
Let t꜀ be the time needed to update one interior point. Each strip owns approximately N²/P points. Therefore:
Tcomp = (N²/P)t꜀
Tcomm / Tcomp = (2tₛ + 2N t𝑤) / [(N²/P)t꜀]
Tcomm / Tcomp = 2P tₛ/(N²t꜀) + 2P t𝑤/(N t꜀)
With P fixed, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term decreases as 1/N. Both approach zero as N increases. Large problems can therefore provide a better balance of computation and communication over a slow network. This does not prove a speedup by itself, since the hardware and MPI implementation also affect performance.
Part 3 report question 1 - Corner ghost values
The explicit five-point stencil computes the next temperature using the center and its four direct neighbors:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r(L + R + B + T)
No diagonal term is present. Even for an owned point at the corner of a block, the required neighbors are in its own block or its adjacent ghost row and column. Hence the corner ghost cells are never read by the stencil and do not need to be exchanged. A nine-point stencil with diagonal terms would require them.
Part 3 report question 2 - Actual process grids
Our non-periodic Cartesian grids use (Py, Px) = (2, 2) for P = 4 and (4, 2) for P = 8. We also consider P = 6, with (Py, Px) = (3, 2), because our three VMs currently have two vCPUs each.
For the busiest strip rank, there are two row messages of length approximately N. For blocks, a rank sends rows of length N/Px and columns of length N/Py to its existing neighbors. We approximate N−1 interior points by N; our actual strip messages contain N+1 doubles.
For P = 4, all ranks have two neighbors: one row and one column exchange. For P = 6 or 8, middle ranks have two row exchanges and one column exchange. These models assume equal link costs and no overlap; they approximate the maximum outgoing cost rather than the full critical path.

Numerical application - Measured network parameters
The Part 0 MPI ping-pong measurements estimated one-way latency from half the round-trip time. We use the heat-2 / heat-3 link as our primary homogeneous-link model:
tₛ = 5.7368 ms; bandwidth B = 4.298 MB/s
t𝑤 = 8/(4.298 × 10⁶) s = 1.86133 µs per double
Example: for N = 2048 and P = 8, using milliseconds throughout:
Tstrips = 2(5.7368) + 2(2048)(0.00186133) = 19.098 ms
Tblocks = 3(5.7368) + 1.25(2048)(0.00186133) = 21.975 ms
Strips are predicted to be faster in this example. For P = 8, the crossover is N > tₛ/(0.75t𝑤) ≈ 4109.46, so blocks are predicted to win at N = 8192.
Required theoretical comparisons (communication only)
Additional predictions for our six-vCPU configuration
Experimental status and limitations
The 72 local comparisons and the two-VM and three-VM Case V correctness tests passed. These small-grid tests establish numerical agreement with the serial solver, not the performance predictions above. The large-grid benchmarks are still pending. With only six vCPUs and no permitted oversubscription, P = 8 cannot currently be measured under the project rules; P = 6 is an additional comparison, not a substitute for the required P = 8 runs.

Numerical Background - Part 2 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Written solutions to Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 of Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Chapter 8 (pp. 24–26). The communication model also prepares Parts 3 and 4.
Task 8.1 - Why not update in place?
(a) Assume that we visit the rows from bottom to top (increasing j), and the points within each row from left to right (increasing i). For an interior point away from physical boundaries, the left neighbour (i−1, j) and the bottom neighbour (i, j−1) have already been updated to level n+1. The right and top neighbours still contain level n values. Fixed boundary values do not change.
(b) No. The explicit scheme requires all five values to come from the old time level:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r[uⁿ(i−1,j) + uⁿ(i+1,j) + uⁿ(i,j−1) + uⁿ(i,j+1)]
Updating in place mixes two time levels. For example, the first updated point can affect the next point during the same sweep. Reversing the sweep changes which neighbours contain new values and can change the numerical result.
(c) Order-independence is essential in parallel because different ranks update their strips concurrently. If the stencil reads partially updated values, the result can depend on the order of operations, the timing of messages and the partition of the grid. With two arrays, every rank reads only level n, writes level n+1, and swaps the arrays at the end of the step. Ghost rows must also contain level n values. The same arithmetic then produces the same result regardless of the order in which points are updated.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
The notes use an ideal N × N grid split evenly among P processes. Assume that N is divisible by P for strips, and that P is a perfect square and N is divisible by √P for square blocks. We count a typical interior rank with all its neighbours. Physical-edge ranks communicate less.
(a) Strips
Each rank owns N/P rows of N values, so it computes N²/P points. It sends one row of N values to each of two neighbours, and receives one row of N values from each.
Sent = 2N numbers; received = 2N numbers; total = 4N numbers.
There are 2 outgoing messages and 2 incoming messages per step (4 individual send/receive events).

Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume (continued)
(b) Square blocks
The ranks form a √P × √P process grid. Each rank owns a square block of side N/√P and area N²/P. An interior rank has four neighbours. The five-point stencil requires only the four edge halos, not diagonal corner messages.
Sent = 4N/√P; received = 4N/√P; total = 8N/√P numbers.
There are 4 outgoing messages and 4 incoming messages per step (8 individual send/receive events).
(c) Communication time per step
The notes give the message model t_msg = tₛ + m t_w, where tₛ is start-up latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t_w is the transfer time per value. We use the usual per-rank model counting one bidirectional exchange per neighbour, with matching send and receive treated as one message cost. We neglect overlap between different neighbour exchanges.
T_comm,strips ≈ 2(tₛ + Nt_w) = 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
T_comm,blocks ≈ 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t_w) = 4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P
If sends and receives are charged separately rather than as paired exchanges, both estimates are doubled; the comparison is unchanged under that convention.
When latency is small, the data volume dominates. Blocks transfer less data than strips for P > 4 in this interior-rank model. When latency is very large, strips are preferable because they require fewer messages.
More precisely, the block estimate is smaller when:
4tₛ + 4Nt_w/√P < 2tₛ + 2Nt_w
tₛ < Nt_w(1 − 2/√P)
Thus blocks need a sufficiently large data volume and a sufficiently low latency to compensate for their additional messages. For small process grids, count the actual neighbours rather than applying the interior-rank formula blindly.
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio for strips
Let γ be the average computation time per point per step. A typical rank owns N²/P points, so:
T_comp ≈ γN²/P
T_comm / T_comp ≈ (2tₛ + 2Nt_w)/(γN²/P)
T_comm / T_comp ≈ 2Ptₛ/(γN²) + 2Pt_w/(γN)
For fixed P, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term as 1/N. Larger grids therefore provide more computation per exchanged value. On a slow network, parallelism is more likely to pay off for large problems, although speedup is not guaranteed by this model alone.

Application to our Part 2 implementation
The project uses N intervals per direction, not exactly the N × N point grid used in Task 8.2. It has (N+1)² total points and (N−1)² updated interior points. The number of rows owned by a rank is determined by the balanced strip partition.
q = ⌊(N−1)/P⌋,     s = (N−1) mod P
n_local(k) = q+1 if k < s; otherwise q.
Each rank stores (n_local+2)(N+1) doubles. The extra rows are ghost rows or physical boundary rows. An actual halo message contains N+1 contiguous doubles (8(N+1) bytes on the tested machines). An interior rank has two MPI neighbours; the first and last ranks have only one when P > 1.
Example: N = 16, P = 3
Here there are 15 interior rows and each rank owns 5. Each rank stores 7 × 17 = 119 doubles per time-level array and updates 5 × 15 = 75 interior temperatures per step. A halo message contains 17 doubles, or 136 bytes.
The three-VM Case V experiment on 24 November 2026 used these parameters, r=0.2 and 10 steps. The measured MPI time was 0.779550588 s, with maximum communication time 0.779543372 s and maximum computation time 0.000008195 s. The serial and distributed fields matched byte for byte. These timings demonstrate communication dominance for this small experiment; they do not establish a general speedup threshold. Timing maxima are independent across ranks.
Connection to the implementation
At every step, MPI_Sendrecv refreshes the ghost rows in the old array before computation. The five-point update writes into the new array, then the arrays are swapped. MPI_Gatherv reconstructs the full field at the end. This implements the order-independence from Task 8.1 and the strip communication pattern from Task 8.2.
Document scope
This document covers both required tasks in Chapter 8. It complements the Part 1 numerical solutions and is not yet the complete project-wide background-notes submission. The final submission must contain all non-optional tasks, numbered as in the notes.
Sources: Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Tasks 8.1 and 8.2 (pp. 24–26); Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale, Section 6 (pp. 7–9); recorded three-VM Case V verification, 24 November 2026.

Numerical Background - Part 3 Solutions
Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale
Task 8.2 (a–d), Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, p. 26; and the two report questions in the project specification, Section 7.
Task 8.2 - Surface-to-volume
(a) Strip decomposition
Consider an N × N grid divided into P horizontal strips. Each process owns N/P rows of N points. A typical interior process has two neighbors. It sends its top and bottom rows and receives one row from each neighbor.
Sent: 2N values in 2 messages; received: 2N values in 2 messages.
In total, it exchanges 4N values in 4 directional messages per step. The amount of computation is proportional to N²/P owned points.
(b) Square block decomposition
For a square process grid, each block has side length N/√P. A typical interior process has four neighbors and sends one row or column to each neighbor. It also receives four corresponding ghost layers.
Sent: 4N/√P values in 4 messages; received: 4N/√P values in 4 messages.
The total exchange is 8N/√P values in 8 directional messages. The computation per process is again proportional to N²/P. These counts assume a process with all four neighbors; boundary ranks have fewer.
(c) Communication time per step
The message model is tₘₛɢ = tₛ + m t𝑤, where tₛ is startup latency, m is the number of transmitted values and t𝑤 is the transfer time per value. We estimate the halo cost using the sum of outgoing message costs, rather than adding a second full cost for simultaneous receives.
Tstrips = 2(tₛ + N t𝑤) = 2tₛ + 2N t𝑤
Tblocks = 4(tₛ + (N/√P)t𝑤) = 4tₛ + (4N/√P)t𝑤
With small latency, square blocks reduce the transfer volume for P > 4. With very large latency, strips have the advantage of fewer messages. Under the typical interior-rank model, blocks are faster when:
tₛ < N t𝑤(1 − 2/√P)
This is a simplified communication model, not a guarantee of actual wall-clock performance. In particular, a non-periodic 2 × 2 grid has no four-neighbor rank.

Task 8.2 (continued)
(d) Communication-to-computation ratio
Let t꜀ be the time needed to update one interior point. Each strip owns approximately N²/P points. Therefore:
Tcomp = (N²/P)t꜀
Tcomm / Tcomp = (2tₛ + 2N t𝑤) / [(N²/P)t꜀]
Tcomm / Tcomp = 2P tₛ/(N²t꜀) + 2P t𝑤/(N t꜀)
With P fixed, the latency term decreases as 1/N² and the transfer term decreases as 1/N. Both approach zero as N increases. Large problems can therefore provide a better balance of computation and communication over a slow network. This does not prove a speedup by itself, since the hardware and MPI implementation also affect performance.
Part 3 report question 1 - Corner ghost values
The explicit five-point stencil computes the next temperature using the center and its four direct neighbors:
uⁿ⁺¹(i,j) = (1 − 4r)uⁿ(i,j) + r(L + R + B + T)
No diagonal term is present. Even for an owned point at the corner of a block, the required neighbors are in its own block or its adjacent ghost row and column. Hence the corner ghost cells are never read by the stencil and do not need to be exchanged. A nine-point stencil with diagonal terms would require them.
Part 3 report question 2 - Actual process grids
Our non-periodic Cartesian grids use (Py, Px) = (2, 2) for P = 4 and (4, 2) for P = 8. We also consider P = 6, with (Py, Px) = (3, 2), because our three VMs currently have two vCPUs each.
For the busiest strip rank, there are two row messages of length approximately N. For blocks, a rank sends rows of length N/Px and columns of length N/Py to its existing neighbors. We approximate N−1 interior points by N; our actual strip messages contain N+1 doubles.
For P = 4, all ranks have two neighbors: one row and one column exchange. For P = 6 or 8, middle ranks have two row exchanges and one column exchange. These models assume equal link costs and no overlap; they approximate the maximum outgoing cost rather than the full critical path.

Numerical application - Measured network parameters
The Part 0 MPI ping-pong measurements estimated one-way latency from half the round-trip time. We use the heat-2 / heat-3 link as our primary homogeneous-link model:
tₛ = 5.7368 ms; bandwidth B = 4.298 MB/s
t𝑤 = 8/(4.298 × 10⁶) s = 1.86133 µs per double
Example: for N = 2048 and P = 8, using milliseconds throughout:
Tstrips = 2(5.7368) + 2(2048)(0.00186133) = 19.098 ms
Tblocks = 3(5.7368) + 1.25(2048)(0.00186133) = 21.975 ms
Strips are predicted to be faster in this example. For P = 8, the crossover is N > tₛ/(0.75t𝑤) ≈ 4109.46, so blocks are predicted to win at N = 8192.
Required theoretical comparisons (communication only)
Additional predictions for our six-vCPU configuration
Experimental status and limitations
The 72 local comparisons and the two-VM and three-VM Case V correctness tests passed. These small-grid tests establish numerical agreement with the serial solver, not the performance predictions above. The large-grid benchmarks are still pending. With only six vCPUs and no permitted oversubscription, P = 8 cannot currently be measured under the project rules; P = 6 is an additional comparison, not a substitute for the required P = 8 runs.
Sources: Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation, Chapter 8, Task 8.2 (p. 26); project specification, Sections 7 and 8.1; team Part 0 latency and bandwidth measurements (23 November 2026).

import json, math, os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import LogLocator, NullFormatter

work = Path(os.environ['WHOLE_NUM_QA'])
roundoff = []
for p in range(1, 11):
    h = 10.0**(-p)
    d2 = (math.sin(1-h) - 2*math.sin(1) + math.sin(1+h))/h**2
    roundoff.append([p, h, abs(d2 + math.sin(1))])

def solve(steps, backward):
    dt = 1.0/steps
    u = 1.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        if backward:
            u /= 1 + 50*dt
        else:
            u *= 1 - 50*dt
    return u

    stability.append([n, dt, 1 - 50*dt, abs(solve(n, False)), solve(n, True)])

    order = math.log2(euler[-1][2]/error) if euler else None
    euler.append([n, 1.0/n, error, order])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.62), layout='constrained')

from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt, RGBColor

qa = Path(os.environ['WHOLE_NUM_QA'])
root = Path.cwd()
desktop = Path('C:/Users/User/Desktop')
results = root / 'part1/results'
data = json.loads((qa/'numerical_data.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))

    convergence_plot = report.read('word/media/image1.png')

    instability_plot = report.read('word/media/image3.png')

sec = doc.sections[0]
sec.page_width, sec.page_height = Inches(8.27), Inches(11.69)
sec.left_margin = sec.right_margin = Inches(.73)
sec.top_margin = sec.bottom_margin = Inches(.63)
doc.core_properties.title = 'Numerical Solutions for the Parallel Heat Diffusion Project'

for name, pts, bold, space_before, space_after in [
    ('Normal', 10.5, False, 0, 5),

]:

    fmt.line_spacing = 1.08 if name == 'Normal' else 1.03
    fmt.widow_control = True
    if name == 'Title' or name.startswith('Heading'):
        fmt.keep_with_next = True

    props = sty.element.get_or_add_pPr()

def body(text):
    return doc.add_paragraph(text)

def heading(text, level=1, page=False):
    p = doc.add_heading(text, level)
    p.paragraph_format.page_break_before = page
    return p

def task(num, title, page=False):
    return heading(f'Task {num} {title}', 2, page)

def eq(text):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(4)
    p.paragraph_format.keep_together = True
    p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Inches(.17)
    for token in re.split(r'([_^]\{[^{}]+\})', text):
        if not token:
            continue
        formatted = token.startswith(('_{','^{'))
        run = p.add_run(token[2:-1] if formatted else token)
        run.font.name = 'Cambria Math'
        if formatted:
            run.font.subscript = token.startswith('_')
            run.font.superscript = token.startswith('^')
    return p

def code(text):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    p.paragraph_format.keep_together = True
    p.paragraph_format.line_spacing = 1.01
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(6)
    run = p.add_run(text)
    run.font.name = 'Consolas'
    run.font.size = Pt(9.2)

def caption(text, before=False):

    p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = before
    return p

def node(parent, tag, **attrs):
    child = OxmlElement('w:'+tag)
    for attr, val in attrs.items():
        child.set(qn('w:'+attr), str(val))
    parent.append(child)
    return child

def table(labels, rows, widths, title=None):
    if title:
        caption(title, before=True)
    t = doc.add_table(rows=0, cols=len(labels))
    t.autofit = False
    t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    for col, width in zip(t.columns, widths):
        col.width = Inches(width)
    p = t._tbl.tblPr
    borders = node(p, 'tblBorders')
    for e in ('top','bottom','left','right','insideH','insideV'):
        node(borders,e,val='single',color='D9D9D9',sz=4)
    margins = node(p,'tblCellMar')
    for e in ('top','bottom','left','right'):
        node(margins,e,w=34 if e in ('top','bottom') else 80,type='dxa')
    for i, row in enumerate([labels, *rows]):
        wr = t.add_row()
        trp = wr._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
        node(trp,'cantSplit')
        if i == 0:
            node(trp,'tblHeader')

            if i == 0:

            run.bold = i == 0
            run.font.size = Pt(9.4)
    return t

def figure(data, width, title, alt):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
    p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(3)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(0)
    source = BytesIO(data) if isinstance(data, bytes) else str(data)
    pic = p.add_run().add_picture(source, width=Inches(width))
    pic._inline.docPr.set('descr',alt)
    caption(title)

def sci(x, digits=4):
    if x == 0:
        return '0'
    a,b = f'{x:.{digits}e}'.split('e')
    return a + ' × 10' + str(int(b)).translate(str.maketrans('-0123456789','⁻⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹'))

def section(n, text, page=True):

body('This is formula (1.2). The radius is written ρ here to distinguish it from the solver parameter r.')

body('(a) Thermal diffusivity α has units m²/s, so αt/L² has units (m²/s)·s/m² = 1.')

body('Let kₓ = mπ/Lₓ, kᵧ = nπ/Lᵧ, and σ = α(kₓ² + kᵧ²). For the mode below, uₜ = −σu, while uₓₓ = −kₓ²u and uᵧᵧ = −kᵧ²u. Hence uₜ = α(uₓₓ + uᵧᵧ).')

section(2, 'Taylor expansions')
task('2.1', 'Expansions at nearby points')
body('All derivatives on the right are evaluated at x. Keep terms through fourth order.')

eq('(c)  f(x+2h) = f(x) + 2hf′ + 2h²f″ + (4h³/3)f‴ + (2h⁴/3)f^{(4)} + O(h⁵).')

section(3, 'Finite differences', page=False)
task('3.1', 'Backward difference')
body('Substitute the expansion of f(x − h) into the numerator and divide by h.')
eq('D₋f(x) = [f(x) − f(x−h)]/h = f′(x) − (h/2)f″(x) + O(h²).')
body('The leading error D₋f − f′ is −(h/2)f″. The backward difference is first-order accurate.')

task('3.2', 'Central second difference')
body('(a–b) Add the expansions at x + h and x − h. The odd terms cancel. After subtracting 2f(x) and dividing by h², the result is')
eq('D₂f(x) = [f(x−h) − 2f(x) + f(x+h)]/h².')
eq('D₂f(x) − f″(x) = (h²/12) f^{(4)}(x) + O(h⁴).')
body('The leading error is proportional to h², so the approximation is second-order accurate.')
body('(c) For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 1, the exact second derivative is −sin(1).')

    (f'{h:g}',f'{e:.9f}',f'{err[i-1]/e:.3f}' if i else '—')
    for i,(h,e) in enumerate(zip(hvals,err))
], (1,1.65,3.04))
body('Halving h reduces the error by about a factor of four, as expected.')

body('(a) A constant gives numerator 1 − 2 + 1 = 0. A linear function gives (x−h) − 2x + (x+h) = 0. For x², the numerator is (x−h)² − 2x² + (x+h)² = 2h², so D₂x² = 2. The formula exactly captures the curvature of these polynomials.')
body('(b) The weights 1, −2, and 1 sum to zero. Adding the same constant to all values leaves the second difference unchanged.')
body('(c) D₂f equals 2/h² times the average of the two neighbors minus the center. A center below the neighboring average gives a positive result.')

section(5, 'Discretizing the heat equation')
task('5.1', 'One dimensional update')
body('(a) For an interior node, use the second difference in the method of lines. The prescribed Dirichlet values supply the end nodes.')
eq('du_{i}/dt = α[u_{i−1} − 2u_{i} + u_{i+1}]/Δx².')
body('(b–c) Forward Euler evaluates that right-hand side at time level n. The dimensionless parameter is r = αΔt/Δx².')
eq('u^{n+1}_{i} = (1 − 2r)u^{n}_{i} + r(u^{n}_{i−1} + u^{n}_{i+1}).')
body('The combination is the same as αt/L² in Task 1.2, now using one time step and one grid spacing.')

task('5.2', 'Two dimensional update')
body('(a) The update at an interior node adds αΔt times the two spatial second differences from Task 3.4, each evaluated at time level n.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = u^{n}(i,j) + αΔt[D_{xx}u^{n}(i,j) + D_{yy}u^{n}(i,j)].')
body('(b) For equal spacing h, set r = αΔt/h². The center weight is 1 − 4r and each neighbor has weight r.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = (1 − 4r)u^{n}(i,j) + r[u^{n}(i−1,j) + u^{n}(i+1,j) + u^{n}(i,j−1) + u^{n}(i,j+1)].')
body('(c) The four neighbors and the center come from the old grid. Only the new center value is written.')
code('Old level n                         New level n + 1\n'
     '          Top\n'
     'Left     Center     Right    ────>        Center\n'
     '         Bottom')
body('(d) With the weights precomputed, summing the four neighbors takes three additions. Two multiplications and one final addition give six floating-point operations per update. Each update uses five input grid values and writes one. Cache reuse reduces the number of memory accesses that reach RAM.')

task('5.3', 'Interpreting the weights')
body('(a) The weights sum to (1 − 4r) + 4r = 1. If the five input values all equal C, the new value remains C. A uniform plate stays uniform when the boundaries are compatible.')
body('(b) The change equals 4r times the four-neighbor average minus the old center value. A warmer neighborhood raises the center temperature. A cooler neighborhood lowers it.')

task('5.4', 'Insulated edges')
body('(a) The left-edge nodes u(0,j) with 1 ≤ j ≤ Nᵧ − 1 are unknowns and are updated. Add one ghost column at x = −Δx. Centering the zero-derivative condition at the wall gives u(−1,j) = u(1,j) at every step.')
body('(b) At a mixed corner, the prescribed Dirichlet value fixes the corner. At a corner joining two insulated edges, the corner is unknown. Mirror the two off-grid cardinal neighbors across their respective walls, then apply the five-point update to the corner.')
body('(c) If the prescribed coordinate derivative is uₓ(0,y,t) = h(t), the centered boundary equation and ghost value are')
eq('[u(1,j) − u(−1,j)]/(2Δx) = h(t),     u(−1,j) = u(1,j) − 2Δx h(t).')

task('5.5', 'Truncation error and consistency', page=True)
body('Substitute the smooth exact solution into the discrete equation. Define τ as the forward time difference minus α times the sum of the centered space differences. Taylor expansion gives')
eq('Forward time difference = u_{t} + (Δt/2)u_{tt} + O(Δt²).')
eq('D_{xx}u = u_{xx} + (Δx²/12)u_{xxxx} + O(Δx⁴).')
eq('D_{yy}u = u_{yy} + (Δy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δy⁴).')
body('The PDE cancels the leading time and space terms. The leading remainder is')
eq('τ = (Δt/2)u_{tt} − (αΔx²/12)u_{xxxx} − (αΔy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δt² + Δx⁴ + Δy⁴).')
body('Thus τ = O(Δt) + O(Δx²) + O(Δy²), so p = 1 and q = 2. The truncation error vanishes as all step sizes shrink. The method is consistent.')

section(6, 'Stability and convergence', page=False)
task('6.1', 'Upwind amplification factor')
body('For the upwind update, G = 1 − ν + ν exp(−iθ) and its conjugate has exp(iθ). Expand their product.')
eq('|G|² = (1−ν)² + ν² + 2ν(1−ν) cos θ.')
eq('        = 1 − 2ν(1−ν)(1−cos θ) = 1 − 4ν(1−ν) sin²(θ/2).')
body('Therefore all modes satisfy |G| ≤ 1 exactly when 0 ≤ ν ≤ 1.')

task('6.2', 'Von Neumann analysis in one dimension')
body('(a) For the mode exp(ijθ) at grid point j, the two neighbors contribute factors exp(±iθ). The amplification factor is real.')
eq('G(θ) = 1 − 2r + 2r cos θ = 1 − 4r sin²(θ/2).')
body('(b) G ranges from 1 − 4r to 1 for r ≥ 0. The zero-frequency mode has |G| = 1. The mode θ = π, with values alternating as (−1)ʲ, has the smallest G and sets the stability limit. It has the largest magnitude if r > 1/2 and ties the zero mode at r = 1/2.')
body('(c) Require 1 − 4r ≥ −1. This gives r ≤ 1/2, or Δt ≤ Δx²/(2α).')

task('6.3', 'Von Neumann analysis in two dimensions')
body('(a) In the mode exp[i(jθ + kφ)], shifts in x and y contribute exp(±iθ) and exp(±iφ). Pairing opposite directions gives')
eq('G = 1 − 4r_{x} sin²(θ/2) − 4r_{y} sin²(φ/2),    r_{x} = αΔt/Δx²,    r_{y} = αΔt/Δy².')
body('(b) The minimum is at θ = φ = π, the checkerboard mode. The maximum is 1. Requiring the minimum to be at least −1 gives')
eq('αΔt(1/Δx² + 1/Δy²) ≤ 1/2.')
body('(c–d) For equal spacing, the bound is r ≤ 1/4 in 2D. Each direction can contribute −4r to G, giving the limits 1/2 in 1D and 1/6 in 3D.')

task('6.4', 'Nonnegative weights and temperature bounds', page=True)
body('The four neighbor weights are the two nonnegative directional values rₓ and rᵧ. The center weight is 1 − 2rₓ − 2rᵧ. All weights are nonnegative when 2(rₓ + rᵧ) ≤ 1, the same bound as Task 6.3. With equal spacing this is r ≤ 1/4.')
body('The weights sum to 1, so under the bound the update is a weighted average. If the center weight is negative, the update can create temperatures outside the old range. For example, a center value 1 surrounded by zeros would become negative.')

task('6.6', 'Counting the work')
body('(a) The grid contains (N+1)² nodes, of which (N−1)² are updated. For α = 1 and h = 1/N, the largest stable step is 1/(4N²). Reaching T = 0.1 takes K = ⌈0.4N²⌉ steps, with the step shortened slightly when needed to reach T exactly.')
body('(b–c) At six operations per interior update, the work is 6K(N−1)² ≈ 2.4N⁴ operations. Doubling N therefore increases the work and the estimated runtime by about 16.')
table(('N','Steps K','Floating-point operations','Time at 10⁹ operations/s'),[
    (f'{n:,}', f'{(2*n*n+4)//5:,}', sci(6*((2*n*n+4)//5)*(n-1)**2), time)
    for n,time in ((1000,'2,395 s (39.9 min)'),(4000,'614,093 s (7.11 days)'))
],(.68,.98,2.16,2.60), '(d) Estimates based on the six-operation stencil count.')

body('The Part 1 Case V run used N = 16 and r = 0.2625, 5% above the limit. The ideal alternating mode has G = 1 − 8r = −1.1. For the finite grid, the highest sine mode has nearly the same checkerboard shape and still has |G| > 1. Its sign flips each step while its amplitude grows.')
body('The error was small at 300 steps. At 400 steps the oscillations are most visible in the plate interior near the center. By 500 steps the error exceeds 1. The snapshots locate the early visible pattern without identifying an exact onset step.')
instability = []
for steps in (100,300,400,500,600,1000):
    log = (results/f'instability_{steps}.txt').read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    err = float(re.search(r'^Max error = (\S+)',log,re.M)[1])
    instability.append((steps,err))
table(('Steps','Max. error','Steps','Max. error'),[
    (f'{a[0]:,}',sci(a[1]),f'{b[0]:,}',sci(b[1]))
    for a,b in zip(instability[:3],instability[3:])
],(1.05,1.85,1.05,1.85), 'Saved maximum absolute errors.')
figure(intermediate_plot,4.93,'Error at 400 and 500 steps. The panels use different color scales.',
       'Two alternating error patterns with the strongest oscillations near the center.')
figure(instability_plot,2.67,'Final temperature field after 1,000 unstable steps.',
       'Checkerboard heat map after 1,000 steps showing alternating large positive and negative temperatures.')
`;

def sci(x, digits=4):
    if x == 0:
        return '0'
    a,b = f'{x:.{digits}e}'.split('e')
    return a + ' × 10' + str(int(b)).translate(str.maketrans('-0123456789','⁻⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹'))

def section(n, text, page=True):
    heading(f'Chapter {n} {text}', page=page)

doc.add_heading('Numerical Solutions for the Parallel Heat Diffusion Project', 0)
body('Parallel 2D Heat Diffusion with MPI over Tailscale')
body('The solutions follow the numbering of Numerical Methods for the Heat Equation. They derive the finite-difference solver, check its stability and accuracy, and apply the communication model to the MPI experiments.')

section(1, 'The physical model', page=False)
task('1.1', 'Mean value formula')
body('Write c = cos φ and s = sin φ. Expand around (x, y), evaluating every derivative at the center.')
eq('u(x + ρc, y + ρs) = u + ρ(cu_{x} + su_{y}) + (ρ²/2)(c²u_{xx} + 2csu_{xy} + s²u_{yy}) + O(ρ³).')
body('Averaging over a full circle gives zero for c, s, and cs, and 1/2 for c² and s². The cubic terms also average to zero because each changes sign when φ is replaced by φ + π. For a smooth u, the remaining error is O(ρ⁴).')
eq('(1/2π)∫_{0}^{2π} u(x + ρ cos φ, y + ρ sin φ) dφ = u(x,y) + (ρ²/4)∇²u(x,y) + O(ρ⁴).')
body('This is formula (1.2). The radius is written ρ here to distinguish it from the solver parameter r.')

task('1.2', 'Diffusion scales')
body('(a) Thermal diffusivity α has units m²/s, so αt/L² has units (m²/s)·s/m² = 1.')
body('(b) In αᵃLᵇ, the time exponent is −a and the length exponent is 2a + b. Setting these to 1 and 0 gives a = −1 and b = 2. The characteristic time is τ = L²/α, multiplied by a dimensionless factor that depends on geometry and the definition of “spread.”')
table(('Material','α (m²/s)','τ for L = 0.10 m'),[
    ('Copper','1.1 × 10⁻⁴','90.9 s'),
    ('Carbon steel','1.3 × 10⁻⁵','769 s'),
],(1.85,1.65,2.20), 'Diffusivities from the background notes.')
body('Copper has the larger diffusivity and the shorter diffusion time. The steel time scale is about 8.5 times as long.')
body('(c) Set x̂ = x/L, ŷ = y/L, and t̂ = αt/L². The chain rule yields the equation below after division by α/L².')
eq('∂u/∂t̂ = ∂²u/∂x̂² + ∂²u/∂ŷ².')
body('A unit-square solver with α = 1 applies to square plates of other sizes and materials when the spatial and time coordinates and the prescribed data are rescaled.')

task('1.3', 'Fourier modes')
body('Let the x and y wave numbers be mπ/Lx and nπ/Ly, respectively. Set the decay rate σ to α times the sum of their squares. Differentiating the mode gives')
eq('u(x,y,t) = sin(k_{x}x) sin(k_{y}y) exp(−σt).')
eq('u_{t} = −σu,    u_{xx} = −k_{x}²u,    u_{yy} = −k_{y}²u,    so u_{t} = α(u_{xx} + u_{yy}).')
body('Each edge makes at least one sine factor zero because m and n are integers. At t = 0 the exponential is 1, leaving the product of the two sines. Case V uses m = n = 1 on the unit square.')

section(2, 'Taylor expansions')
task('2.1', 'Expansions at nearby points')
body('All derivatives on the right are evaluated at x. Keep terms through fourth order.')
eq('(a)  f(x+h) = f(x) + hf′ + (h²/2)f″ + (h³/6)f‴ + (h⁴/24)f^{(4)} + O(h⁵).')
eq('(b)  f(x−h) = f(x) − hf′ + (h²/2)f″ − (h³/6)f‴ + (h⁴/24)f^{(4)} + O(h⁵).')
body('The odd powers change sign because replacing h by −h multiplies the kth term by (−1)ᵏ.')
eq('(c)  f(x+2h) = f(x) + 2hf′ + 2h²f″ + (4h³/3)f‴ + (2h⁴/3)f^{(4)} + O(h⁵).')

section(3, 'Finite differences', page=False)
task('3.1', 'Backward difference')
body('Substitute the expansion of f(x − h) into the numerator and divide by h.')
eq('D₋f(x) = [f(x) − f(x−h)]/h = f′(x) − (h/2)f″(x) + O(h²).')
body('The leading error D₋f − f′ is −(h/2)f″. The backward difference is first-order accurate.')

task('3.2', 'Central second difference')
body('(a–b) Add the expansions at x + h and x − h. The odd terms cancel. After subtracting 2f(x) and dividing by h², the result is')
eq('D₂f(x) = [f(x−h) − 2f(x) + f(x+h)]/h².')
eq('D₂f(x) − f″(x) = (h²/12) f^{(4)}(x) + O(h⁴).')
body('The leading error is proportional to h², so the approximation is second-order accurate.')
body('(c) For f(x) = sin(x) at x = 1, the exact second derivative is −sin(1).')
hvals = (0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125)
err = [abs((math.sin(1-h) - 2*math.sin(1) + math.sin(1+h))/h**2 + math.sin(1)) for h in hvals]
table(('h','Absolute error','Previous error ÷ current error'),[
    (f'{h:g}',f'{e:.9f}',f'{err[i-1]/e:.3f}' if i else '—')
    for i,(h,e) in enumerate(zip(hvals,err))
], (1,1.65,3.04))
body('Halving h reduces the error by about a factor of four, as expected.')

task('3.3', 'Checks on the formula')
body('(a) A constant gives numerator 1 − 2 + 1 = 0. A linear function gives (x−h) − 2x + (x+h) = 0. For x², the numerator is (x−h)² − 2x² + (x+h)² = 2h², so D₂x² = 2. The formula exactly captures the curvature of these polynomials.')
body('(b) The weights 1, −2, and 1 sum to zero. Adding the same constant to all values leaves the second difference unchanged.')
body('(c) D₂f equals 2/h² times the average of the two neighbors minus the center. A center below the neighboring average gives a positive result.')

task('3.4', 'Discrete Laplacian', page=True)
body('(a–c) Apply the centered second difference along each coordinate. Their sum approximates ∇²u with truncation error O(Δx² + Δy²).')
eq('D_{xx}u = [u(i−1,j) − 2u(i,j) + u(i+1,j)] / Δx².')
eq('D_{yy}u = [u(i,j−1) − 2u(i,j) + u(i,j+1)] / Δy².')
body('(d–e) When Δx = Δy = h, the Laplacian uses the following weights with a common factor 1/h².')
code('                 +1\n'
     '          +1     −4     +1\n'
     '                 +1')
body('(f) This is 4/h² times the four-neighbor average minus the center. Like the continuous mean-value formula, it gives a positive Laplacian when the surrounding values are warmer than the center.')

task('3.5', 'Round off and grid spacing')
body('We evaluated the three-point formula for sin(x) at x = 1 using double-precision arithmetic. The experiment is reproduced by the following Python loop.')
code('from math import sin\n'
     'for k in range(1, 11):\n'
     '    h = 10.0**(-k)\n'
     '    d2 = (sin(1-h) - 2*sin(1) + sin(1+h)) / h**2\n'
     '    print(h, abs(d2 + sin(1)))')
roundoff = data['roundoff']
table(('h','Absolute error','h','Absolute error'),[
    (sci(a[1],0),sci(a[2]),sci(b[1],0),sci(b[2]))
    for a,b in zip(roundoff[:5],roundoff[5:])
],(1.05,2.0,1.05,2.0), 'Measured errors for the ten spacings.')
figure(qa/'roundoff.png', 6.37, 'The smallest sampled error occurs at h = 10⁻⁴.',
       'Log-log plot showing falling truncation error and rising round-off error as h decreases.')
body('The truncation term scales as h². The subtraction in the numerator loses precision, leaving an error of order ε that is divided by h². Balancing h² and ε/h² gives h of order ε¹ᐟ⁴, about 10⁻⁴ in double precision. Below this, cancellation dominates and the individual errors fluctuate.')

section(4, 'Time discretization')
task('4.1', 'Forward and backward Euler')
body('(a) For u′ = −50u with u(0) = 1, the exact value at t = 1 is exp(−50). We used K steps with Δt = 1/K and iterated both updates in Python.')
code('def euler(steps, backward=False):\n'
     '    dt = 1.0 / steps\n'
     '    u = 1.0\n'
     '    for _ in range(steps):\n'
     '        u = u / (1 + 50*dt) if backward else (1 - 50*dt)*u\n'
     '    return u')
body('(b) Forward Euler multiplies u by 1 − 50Δt. Its magnitude is bounded if that multiplier lies in [−1, 1]. The largest stable step is 0.04. At equality the values alternate between ±1. At K = 24 and K = 20 the magnitudes grow.')
table(('Steps K','Δt','Forward multiplier','Forward |u(1)|','Backward u(1)'),[
    (n, f'{dt:.6f}', f'{g:.6f}', f'{value:.6g}', sci(be,3)) for n,dt,g,value,be in data['stability']
],(.82,1.00,1.68,1.37,1.59),'Stability runs with both updates.')
body('(c) For the finer steps below, we measured the absolute error at t = 1. The observed order log₂(E(Δt)/E(Δt/2)) approaches 1.')
table(('Steps K','Δt','Absolute error at t = 1','Observed order'),[
    (f'{n:,}',sci(dt,3),sci(e),f'{order:.4f}' if order else '—') for n,dt,e,order in data['euler']
],(1.07,1.30,2.02,1.49))
figure(qa/'euler.png',5.85,'The forward Euler errors approach the reference slope of 1.',
       'Log-log plot showing first-order convergence in the forward Euler time step.')
body('(d) Backward Euler gives uⁿ⁺¹ = uⁿ/(1 + 50Δt). The measured values decay even for steps above the forward Euler threshold. Its multiplier is strictly between 0 and 1 for every Δt > 0, so decay holds for any positive time step.')

section(5, 'Discretizing the heat equation')
task('5.1', 'One dimensional update')
body('(a) For an interior node, use the second difference in the method of lines. The prescribed Dirichlet values supply the end nodes.')
eq('du_{i}/dt = α[u_{i−1} − 2u_{i} + u_{i+1}]/Δx².')
body('(b–c) Forward Euler evaluates that right-hand side at time level n. The dimensionless parameter is r = αΔt/Δx².')
eq('u^{n+1}_{i} = (1 − 2r)u^{n}_{i} + r(u^{n}_{i−1} + u^{n}_{i+1}).')
body('The combination is the same as αt/L² in Task 1.2, now using one time step and one grid spacing.')

task('5.2', 'Two dimensional update')
body('(a) The update at an interior node adds αΔt times the two spatial second differences from Task 3.4, each evaluated at time level n.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = u^{n}(i,j) + αΔt[D_{xx}u^{n}(i,j) + D_{yy}u^{n}(i,j)].')
body('(b) For equal spacing h, set r = αΔt/h². The center weight is 1 − 4r and each neighbor has weight r.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = (1 − 4r)u^{n}(i,j) + r[u^{n}(i−1,j) + u^{n}(i+1,j) + u^{n}(i,j−1) + u^{n}(i,j+1)].')
body('(c) The four neighbors and the center come from the old grid. Only the new center value is written.')
code('Old level n                         New level n + 1\n'
     '          Top\n'
     'Left     Center     Right    ────>        Center\n'
     '         Bottom')
body('(d) With the weights precomputed, summing the four neighbors takes three additions. Two multiplications and one final addition give six floating-point operations per update. Each update uses five input grid values and writes one. Cache reuse reduces the number of memory accesses that reach RAM.')

task('5.3', 'Interpreting the weights')
body('(a) The weights sum to (1 − 4r) + 4r = 1. If the five input values all equal C, the new value remains C. A uniform plate stays uniform when the boundaries are compatible.')
body('(b) The change equals 4r times the four-neighbor average minus the old center value. A warmer neighborhood raises the center temperature. A cooler neighborhood lowers it.')

task('5.4', 'Insulated edges')
body('(a) The left-edge nodes between the two corners are unknowns and are updated. Add one ghost column at x = −Δx. Centering the zero-derivative condition at the wall gives u(−1,j) = u(1,j) at every step.')
body('(b) At a mixed corner, the prescribed Dirichlet value fixes the corner. At a corner joining two insulated edges, the corner is unknown. Mirror the two off-grid cardinal neighbors across their respective walls, then apply the five-point update to the corner.')
body('(c) If the prescribed coordinate derivative is uₓ(0,y,t) = h(t), the centered boundary equation and ghost value are')
eq('[u(1,j) − u(−1,j)]/(2Δx) = h(t),     u(−1,j) = u(1,j) − 2Δx h(t).')

task('5.5', 'Truncation error and consistency', page=True)
body('Substitute the smooth exact solution into the discrete equation. Define τ as the forward time difference minus α times the sum of the centered space differences. Taylor expansion gives')
eq('Forward time difference = u_{t} + (Δt/2)u_{tt} + O(Δt²).')
eq('D_{xx}u = u_{xx} + (Δx²/12)u_{xxxx} + O(Δx⁴).')
eq('D_{yy}u = u_{yy} + (Δy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δy⁴).')
body('The PDE cancels the leading time and space terms. The leading remainder is')
eq('τ = (Δt/2)u_{tt} − (αΔx²/12)u_{xxxx} − (αΔy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δt² + Δx⁴ + Δy⁴).')
body('Thus τ = O(Δt) + O(Δx²) + O(Δy²), so p = 1 and q = 2. The truncation error vanishes as all step sizes shrink. The method is consistent.')

section(6, 'Stability and convergence', page=False)
task('6.1', 'Upwind amplification factor')
body('For the upwind update, G = 1 − ν + ν exp(−iθ) and its conjugate has exp(iθ). Expand their product.')
eq('|G|² = (1−ν)² + ν² + 2ν(1−ν) cos θ.')
eq('        = 1 − 2ν(1−ν)(1−cos θ) = 1 − 4ν(1−ν) sin²(θ/2).')
body('Therefore all modes satisfy |G| ≤ 1 exactly when 0 ≤ ν ≤ 1.')

task('6.2', 'Von Neumann analysis in one dimension')
body('(a) For the mode exp(ijθ) at grid point j, the two neighbors contribute factors exp(±iθ). The amplification factor is real.')
eq('G(θ) = 1 − 2r + 2r cos θ = 1 − 4r sin²(θ/2).')
body('(b) G ranges from 1 − 4r to 1 for r ≥ 0. The zero-frequency mode has |G| = 1. The mode θ = π, with values alternating as (−1)ʲ, has the smallest G and sets the stability limit. It has the largest magnitude if r > 1/2 and ties the zero mode at r = 1/2.')
body('(c) Require 1 − 4r ≥ −1. This gives r ≤ 1/2, or Δt ≤ Δx²/(2α).')

task('6.3', 'Von Neumann analysis in two dimensions')
body('(a) In the mode exp[i(jθ + kφ)], shifts in x and y contribute exp(±iθ) and exp(±iφ). Pairing opposite directions gives')
eq('G = 1 − 4r_{x} sin²(θ/2) − 4r_{y} sin²(φ/2),    r_{x} = αΔt/Δx²,    r_{y} = αΔt/Δy².')
body('(b) The minimum is at θ = φ = π, the checkerboard mode. The maximum is 1. Requiring the minimum to be at least −1 gives')
eq('αΔt(1/Δx² + 1/Δy²) ≤ 1/2.')
body('(c–d) For equal spacing, the bound is r ≤ 1/4 in 2D. Each direction can contribute −4r to G, giving the limits 1/2 in 1D and 1/6 in 3D.')

task('6.4', 'Nonnegative weights and temperature bounds', page=True)
body('Each horizontal neighbor has weight rx and each vertical neighbor has weight ry, as defined in Task 6.3. The center weight is 1 − 2(rx + ry). All weights are nonnegative when 2(rx + ry) ≤ 1, the same bound as Task 6.3. For equal spacings this is r ≤ 1/4.')
body('The weights sum to 1, so under the bound the update is a weighted average. If the center weight is negative, the update can create temperatures outside the old range. For example, a center value 1 surrounded by zeros would become negative.')

task('6.6', 'Counting the work')
body('(a) The grid contains (N+1)² nodes, of which (N−1)² are updated. For α = 1 and h = 1/N, the largest stable step is 1/(4N²). Reaching T = 0.1 takes K = ⌈0.4N²⌉ steps, with the step shortened slightly when needed to reach T exactly.')
body('(b–c) At six operations per interior update, the work is 6K(N−1)² ≈ 2.4N⁴ operations. Doubling N therefore increases the work and the estimated runtime by about 16.')
table(('N','Steps K','Floating-point operations','Time at 10⁹ operations/s'),[
    (f'{n:,}', f'{(2*n*n+4)//5:,}', sci(6*((2*n*n+4)//5)*(n-1)**2), time)
    for n,time in ((1000,'2,395 s (39.9 min)'),(4000,'614,093 s (7.11 days)'))
],(.68,.98,2.16,2.60), '(d) Estimates based on the six-operation stencil count.')

task('6.7', 'Deliberate instability')
body('The Part 1 Case V run used N = 16 and r = 0.2625, 5% above the limit. The ideal alternating mode has G = 1 − 8r = −1.1. For the finite grid, the highest sine mode has nearly the same checkerboard shape and still has |G| > 1. Its sign flips each step while its amplitude grows.')
body('The error was small at 300 steps. At 400 steps the oscillations are most visible in the plate interior near the center. By 500 steps the error exceeds 1. The snapshots locate the early visible pattern without identifying an exact onset step.')
instability = []
for steps in (100,300,400,500,600,1000):
    log = (results/f'instability_{steps}.txt').read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    err = float(re.search(r'^Max error = (\S+)',log,re.M)[1])
    instability.append((steps,err))
table(('Steps','Max. error','Steps','Max. error'),[
    (f'{a[0]:,}',sci(a[1]),f'{b[0]:,}',sci(b[1]))
    for a,b in zip(instability[:3],instability[3:])
],(1.05,1.85,1.05,1.85), 'Saved maximum absolute errors.')
figure(intermediate_plot,4.93,'Error at 400 and 500 steps. The panels use different color scales.',
       'Two alternating error patterns with the strongest oscillations near the center.')
figure(instability_plot,2.67,'Final temperature field after 1,000 unstable steps.',
       'Checkerboard heat map after 1,000 steps showing alternating large positive and negative temperatures.')

section(7, 'Verifying the solver')
task('7.1', 'Expected convergence order')
body('Task 5.5 gives a time term of order Δt and a space term of order h². With r fixed, Δt = rh²/α, so both terms scale as h². For this stable, smooth case we expect order two in h. Halving h should reduce the error by about four.')

task('7.2', 'Case V convergence study')
body('(a) The serial solver used Case V with α = 1, T = 0.05, and r = 0.2 at N = 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256. The step count T/(rh²) was an integer on each grid.')
body('(b) At the final time, compare the numerical field with sin(πx) sin(πy) exp(−2π²T). We measure the maximum nodal error and the discrete L₂ error, which is h times the square root of the sum of squared nodal errors.')
with (results/'convergence.csv').open(newline='',encoding='utf-8') as fp:
    convergence = list(csv.DictReader(fp))
table(('N','h','Steps','Maximum error','Discrete L₂ error','Observed order'),[
    (row['N'],f"1/{row['N']}",f"{int(row['steps']):,}",sci(float(row['max_error']),5),
     sci(float(row['l2h_error']),5),f"{float(row['p_obs']):.4f}" if row['p_obs'] else '—')
    for row in convergence
],(.54,.62,.81,1.55,1.63,1.35),'Saved serial results at T = 0.05.')
figure(convergence_plot,6.35,'Log-log plot of the two errors against h. The reference line has slope 2.',
       'The maximum error and the discrete L2 error both decline with approximately second-order slope.')
body('(c) Using p = log₂[E(h)/E(h/2)] for the discrete L₂ error, the measured order changes from 2.0058 to 2.0001 across the refinements. This agrees with Task 7.1.')

section(8, 'From the scheme to MPI')
task('8.1', 'Why two time levels are needed')
body('(a) In a row-by-row sweep with increasing i and j, an interior point’s left and bottom neighbors have already been visited and contain level n + 1. Its right and top neighbors still contain level n. Fixed boundary values stay fixed.')
body('(b) The five-point forward Euler formula requires all input values at level n. Overwriting values in place instead mixes levels, and reversing the sweep changes which neighbors have already been updated.')
body('(c) With MPI, the mixed time levels could also depend on rank ownership and the order in which halos arrive. Separate old and new arrays let every rank read only level n, including its halos, and write only level n + 1. Swapping the arrays preserves the serial calculation for every partition.')

task('8.2', 'Surface to volume and halo costs')
body('Use the ideal N × N point grid and a typical interior rank. The square-block case assumes a square process grid. Each rank updates about N²/P values per step.')
table(('Decomposition','Values sent','Values received','Messages sent / received'),[
    ('(a) Strips','2N','2N','2 / 2'),
    ('(b) Square blocks','4N/√P','4N/√P','4 / 4'),
], (1.75,1.22,1.25,2.32), 'Per interior rank per time step.')
body('A strip has two neighboring rows of N values. A square block has four sides of N/√P values. The five-point stencil uses only these row and column halos. A stencil with diagonal terms, such as the nine-point stencil, would also need the corner values.')
body('(c) With a startup cost tₛ and a transfer cost per value, budget one message cost per neighbor, treating the paired send and receive as one exchange in this simple estimate.')
eq('T_{strips} ≈ 2t_{s} + 2N t_{w},     T_{blocks} ≈ 4t_{s} + (4N/√P)t_{w}.')
body('When latency is small, blocks have the smaller data volume for P > 4. When latency dominates, strips benefit from fewer messages. The interior-rank model favors blocks when the startup cost satisfies the inequality below.')
eq('t_{s} < N t_{w}(1 − 2/√P).')
body('(d) If γ is the computation time per update, the strip computation cost is about γN²/P. The ratio becomes')
eq('T_{comm}/T_{comp} ≈ 2P t_{s}/(γN²) + 2P t_{w}/(γN).')
body('At fixed P the latency term falls like 1/N², and the transfer term falls like 1/N. Larger grids offer more computation per exchanged value, which makes parallelism easier to justify on a slow network.')

heading('Application to the measured MPI cluster',page=True)
body('The project uses N intervals, so it updates (N−1)² interior points. In strips, the N−1 rows are split as evenly as possible. One actual row message contains N+1 doubles. For example, at N = 16 and P = 3, each rank owns five interior rows and sends 17 doubles per neighboring rank. The middle rank has two neighbors and each end rank has one.')

body('For the project’s nonperiodic blocks, count only existing neighbors. Rows have approximate length N divided by the process-grid width, and columns have length N divided by its height. The busiest ranks give the following approximate outgoing costs.')
table(('Configuration','Messages','Values sent','Communication cost per step'),[
    ('Strips, P ≥ 3','2','2N','2tₛ + 2Nt_w'),
    ('Blocks, P = 4','2','N','2tₛ + Nt_w'),
    ('Blocks, P = 6','3','4N/3','3tₛ + (4N/3)t_w'),
    ('Blocks, P = 8','3','5N/4','3tₛ + (5N/4)t_w'),
],(1.46,1.02,1.13,2.89))
body('Using the Part 0 heat-2 to heat-3 ping-pong fit gives 5.7368 ms startup and 4.2975 MB/s effective bandwidth. An eight-byte double then costs about 1.8615 µs to transfer. The table uses the same link cost for every exchange as a simplifying assumption.')

with (root/'part0/results/network_summary.csv').open(newline='',encoding='utf-8') as fp:
    link = next(r for r in csv.DictReader(fp) if r['connection']=='heat2_heat3_direct')
ts = float(link['latency_ms'])
tw = 1000*8/(float(link['bandwidth_MB_s'])*1e6)
network_rows = []
for processes, msgs, length in ((4,2,1), (8,3,1.25)):

section(5, 'Discretizing the heat equation')
task('5.1', 'One dimensional update')
body('(a) For an interior node, use the second difference in the method of lines. The prescribed Dirichlet values supply the end nodes.')
eq('du_{i}/dt = α[u_{i−1} − 2u_{i} + u_{i+1}]/Δx².')
body('(b–c) Forward Euler evaluates that right-hand side at time level n. The dimensionless parameter is r = αΔt/Δx².')
eq('u^{n+1}_{i} = (1 − 2r)u^{n}_{i} + r(u^{n}_{i−1} + u^{n}_{i+1}).')
body('The combination is the same as αt/L² in Task 1.2, now using one time step and one grid spacing.')

task('5.2', 'Two dimensional update')
body('(a) The update at an interior node adds αΔt times the two spatial second differences from Task 3.4, each evaluated at time level n.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = u^{n}(i,j) + αΔt[D_{xx}u^{n}(i,j) + D_{yy}u^{n}(i,j)].')
body('(b) For equal spacing h, set r = αΔt/h². The center weight is 1 − 4r and each neighbor has weight r.')
eq('u^{n+1}(i,j) = (1 − 4r)u^{n}(i,j) + r[u^{n}(i−1,j) + u^{n}(i+1,j) + u^{n}(i,j−1) + u^{n}(i,j+1)].')
body('(c) The four neighbors and the center come from the old grid. Only the new center value is written.')
code('Old level n                         New level n + 1\n'
     '          Top\n'
     'Left     Center     Right    ────>        Center\n'
     '         Bottom')
body('(d) With the weights precomputed, summing the four neighbors takes three additions. Two multiplications and one final addition give six floating-point operations per update. Each update uses five input grid values and writes one. Cache reuse reduces the number of memory accesses that reach RAM.')

task('5.3', 'Interpreting the weights')
body('(a) The weights sum to (1 − 4r) + 4r = 1. If the five input values all equal C, the new value remains C. A uniform plate stays uniform when the boundaries are compatible.')
body('(b) The change equals 4r times the four-neighbor average minus the old center value. A warmer neighborhood raises the center temperature. A cooler neighborhood lowers it.')

task('5.4', 'Insulated edges')
body('(a) The left-edge nodes between the two corners are unknowns and are updated. Add one ghost column at x = −Δx. Centering the zero-derivative condition at the wall gives u(−1,j) = u(1,j) at every step.')
body('(b) At a mixed corner, the prescribed Dirichlet value fixes the corner. At a corner joining two insulated edges, the corner is unknown. Mirror the two off-grid cardinal neighbors across their respective walls, then apply the five-point update to the corner.')
body('(c) If the prescribed coordinate derivative is uₓ(0,y,t) = h(t), the centered boundary equation and ghost value are')
eq('[u(1,j) − u(−1,j)]/(2Δx) = h(t),     u(−1,j) = u(1,j) − 2Δx h(t).')

task('5.5', 'Truncation error and consistency', page=True)
body('Substitute the smooth exact solution into the discrete equation. Define τ as the forward time difference minus α times the sum of the centered space differences. Taylor expansion gives')
eq('Forward time difference = u_{t} + (Δt/2)u_{tt} + O(Δt²).')
eq('D_{xx}u = u_{xx} + (Δx²/12)u_{xxxx} + O(Δx⁴).')
eq('D_{yy}u = u_{yy} + (Δy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δy⁴).')
body('The PDE cancels the leading time and space terms. The leading remainder is')
eq('τ = (Δt/2)u_{tt} − (αΔx²/12)u_{xxxx} − (αΔy²/12)u_{yyyy} + O(Δt² + Δx⁴ + Δy⁴).')
body('Thus τ = O(Δt) + O(Δx²) + O(Δy²), so p = 1 and q = 2. The truncation error vanishes as all step sizes shrink. The method is consistent.')

body('For the upwind update, G = 1 − ν + ν exp(−iθ) and its conjugate has exp(iθ). Expand their product.')
eq('|G|² = (1−ν)² + ν² + 2ν(1−ν) cos θ.')
eq('        = 1 − 2ν(1−ν)(1−cos θ) = 1 − 4ν(1−ν) sin²(θ/2).')
body('Therefore all modes satisfy |G| ≤ 1 exactly when 0 ≤ ν ≤ 1.')

eq('G(θ) = 1 − 2r + 2r cos θ = 1 − 4r sin²(θ/2).')
body('(b) G ranges from 1 − 4r to 1 for r ≥ 0. The zero-frequency mode has |G| = 1. The mode θ = π, with values alternating as (−1)ʲ, has the smallest G and sets the stability limit. It has the largest magnitude if r > 1/2 and ties the zero mode at r = 1/2.')
